MR. DIEFENBAKER-REPORT IN' OTTAWA "CITIZEN" OF SPEECH MADE TO CANADIAN WEEKLY NEWSPAPERS ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege in regard to a press report in today's issue of the Ottawa Citizen. This is the first time I have ever had to rise on a question of privilege with regard to a newspaper report. The Ottawa Citizen of today's issue reports that when I spoke last evening to the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association I stated in part as follow's:
Canadian citizenship knows only one language and one loyalty.	.
That portion of the report is incorrect in its entirety; for never was the matter discussed by me or anything said that could be subject to such an interpretation, and much less is the alleged quotation justified. Six members from this side of the house, as well as the hon. member for Matapedia-Matane (Mr. Cote) and the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), were present on the occasion, and I know that they will bear me out that such a statement was not made by me, nor did I use certain of the other words ascribed to me in the following paragraph:
All that now remains is for us to remember in our hearts the need for equality of rights, a realization of our responsibilities and equality before the law to assure the preservation of the principles of democracy, without regard to the influence of any race, tongue or creed.
The words "without regard to the influence of" or "tongue" or words to that effect were not used by me. What I stated was that all of us must realize our responsibilities as Canadians and that democracy can only be preserved under equality under law and equality of rights for all Canadians without regard to race or creed.

I am not sure that action will be taken regarding the contract with the Dominion Coal Company. It is a continuing contract and unless it can be altered it binds the government to pay the loss of the company up to March 31 next.

The house resumed from Thursday, February 20, consideration in committee of Bill No. 17, respecting supplemental payments on mail contracts-Mr. Bertrand (Laurier)-Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

Last night the minister said that he would have officials of his department with him today and would be able to answer questions and perhaps tell us the basis for these war-time and operational bonuses.

I have here a statement with regard to five contractors, and this will pretty well explain how the bonuses were granted.
The first is Douro No. 1. It is six trips per week. The distance is 13-8 miles. The contract rate is $475. The bonus granted was $50, and in this case the rate per mile with the bonus became $38.04. In this case $50 was asked for and it was granted because it was very reasonable in the circumstances, making the rate per mile $38.04.
For Ennismore No. 2, and this is in July, 1945, there were six trips per week; the distance was 17[DOT] 3 miles; the contract rate was $560. We gave a bonus of $140, making the rate per mile with bonus $40.46. There is a slight difference in the per mile rate here. The route is longer than the Douro route, and the contractor asked for an increase of $140, which we thought was reasonable. In order to see what should be granted we compared the rate per mile with the other rates per mile in the vicinity and compared the difficulties of the road and so on, and a rate of $40.46 per mile was granted.
In July, 1943, Keene No. 2: six trips per week; distance, 22-9 miles; contract rate $575; bonus granted, $275, making a rate per mile with bonus of $37.12. In this case the contractor asked for a specific amount of $275, which we granted, because we thought it was reasonable. Hon. members can see by comparing it with the rates in the vicinity that it was about the same, and it surely was not too high. I will admit that.
It was not high enough.

In December 1946, Peterborough No. 1, six trips per week, 47-8 miles; the contract rate, $1,300. The contractor asked for a specific amount of $360, making a per mile rate of $34.73. Of

Postal Service
course we granted it. The rate was reasonable at the time it was granted but, without bonus, the contractor would not have been able to carry on his work.
In March, 1945, Peterborough No. 4, again six trips per week, 34-4 miles, contract rate, $1,200; we granted a bonus of S200, making a per mile rate of $40.70. In view of the many factors to be considered, such as frequency, mileage, equipment, hours of service, character of terrain, severity of winters, the condition of the roads and so forth, no formula equitable to all has been devised or can be devised. Each case is dealt with on its merits.
I might remind the house that a short route of eight or nine miles should justify a higher mileage rate than a route of say thirty miles. The reason is that service over a short route requires only a short period of time but the hours of service might be such as to interfere with the contractor's prospects of securing other remunerative work. But on long routes the contractors have the prospect of adding to their income by carrying passengers, freight, and so forth. This fact is generally reflected in the tenders received and increases the difficulty of devising a formula which would be fair in all cases.
In order to determine whether we should grant a bonus we take the tenders that have been asked for over the same route and we sometimes find, as we did in one of these contracts, that the amount of the lowest tender was exactly the amount which the contractor was asking as a bonus, and which according to our experience would have been a fair and reasonable amount for the contract.
Does the minister not feel that that average rate per mile of $40.46 is extremely low for a route of that kind? These roads are pretty tough going.

We have
granted the bonus only where it was necessary and we felt that the contractor was not able to carry on without the bonus on account of the difficulties in abnormal times. But as a rule we are limited by the tenders. We have to accept the lowest tender when the tenderer is able to fulfil his contract. We cannot be blamed if contractors set a -lowr price in their tenders. But it would have been worse if we had kept them to the price of their tenders, because it would have meant that a lot of routes would have had to be abandoned or new tenders called.

Suppose a rural mail contractor comes to the department and asks for a bonus on account of the extremely high cost of living-and despite what the statistical department says about the cost of living having
gone up about 26 per cent it has actually gone up 70 per cent or more-what do you do in that case? Is an inspector sent to check on the roads, or what procedure is followed?

First of all we would compare the price paid with prices paid in the vicinity, and we would send an inspector to verify what the contractor has told us about the road, and so forth. If we think that the bonus asked for is too high, we tell the contractor: If you want to quit we will call for new tenders. Then we make a temporary arrangement. We call for tenders, and often we find that in these days the new tenders are higher than the bonus that has been asked for. That is why we are asking for this legislation, which is to be of a temporary character because in a year from now we shall have to ask for new tenders when the time comes to renew the contracts. The bonus was granted to help these contractors. If we were to ask for new tenders, the prices would be much higher because a new contractor would have to get the necessary equipment.
Does not the minister feel that a number of these contractors hesitate to ask for a bonus for fear the contract might be taken away from them?

No. When they ask for a bonus we either grant it or we do not. But no resentment is held against them at all. We are very glad when the circumstances enable us to give the bonus. I would not be introducing this legislation if it were to be permanent legislation. My officials, as a matter of fact, thought that we should have asked for this power two years ago. But I said no, and it is now being asked for one year only.

Let me give just one case to show the low rate that these men are getting. This contractor has to cover twenty-two miles six times a week, and the contract rate is $862.57. There is no bonus paid. That figures out at about $2.68 for a trip of 22 miles. That is a pretty low rate. A man cannot do it and pay for tires and gasoline at their present high prices.

It is pretty difficult for me to answer without knowing all the details, which I have not here. We would have to know when the contract was granted, because conditions were very different before the war.

This contract was evidently renewed.
Postal Service

If it was renewed the contractor must have been satisfied. The Postmaster General's department is not a department which is running after people to give them a bonus. We give the bonus only when we are satisfied that it is justified.

Since this bill first came before the house I have had occasions to look over the picture so far as rural routes in Canada are concerned, and I feel that if many of the members had looked over the rural route situation apart from their own constituencies, many of the statements which have been made would not have been made.
First of all I think that every hon. member is agreed that the granting of the bonus was a splendid thing. I have never heard a word of complaint about it. I was one of those who advocated that the bonus should be given because, as is well known, many contractors had tendered at far too low a rate. The bonus was granted to every rural mail carrier in my constituency.
Some do not get it.

I will tell you in a moment why some do not get it. It may surprise some members to learn that in the constituency of New Westminster there are more householders receiving rural mail than in the whole of Saskatchewan, and the number is equal to the number receiving rural mail in the whole of Manitoba. I was surprised also to learn that on some of the rural routes there are as few as eleven people receiving rural mail, whilst in the constituency of New Westminster there are rural mail routes serving 651 people. Does any hon. member realize the difference between serving eleven persons and serving 651 in one day? The man who serves the 651 householders has to be at his job two or three hours ahead of time in order to sort out the mail. As a matter of fact the postmaster in New Westminster has often to supply help, and I have known of instances in which the mail has been so heavy for the 651 householders that two trips per day had to be made.
Looking over the whole list one finds that some rural mail carriers make one trip per week while others make two trips, others three, four or five. Hon. members talk about putting this on an equal basis throughout the country, but taking the entire picture as presented by the Post Office department-I dug it up the other day-one is at a loss to understand the statements of certain hon. members of the opposition.

I believe we all have at heart the interests of the mail carriers, but I suggest that the prices which are being paid now show a new trend in the submission of contract prices. The latest in my district averages $81.54 a mile. If one considers it only from the standpoint of mileage, or of roads-whether they be gravel or otherwise-and overlooks the number of householders, he is not dealing with the question in its entirety. Hon. members have not touched upon the number of householders served or the number of trips made.
I thought I would draw the attention of hon. members to these facts so that we might deal with the matter as a whole and see the whole picture. I cannot see the justice in placing a man who calls on only eleven persons once a week on the same footing and paying him the same price as the rural mail carrier who travels six days each week, serving 651 householders each day. I have risen particularly to support the government in the granting of these bonuses, although I can see some difficulty in giving bonuses to everyone. Why should a bonus be given to a man who serves only eleven householders? But in British Columbia nearly everyone who has applied, so far as I know, has received the wartime bonus, and with that I am in hearty accord.
Is the rural mail contractor who serves 651 householders operating on foot or by automobile?
He operates by motor car. He could never carry on his back the mail for 651 householders.

How could he possibly
make that many stops in a day?

I don't know, but you had
better take a lesson from him; because they do it out there, and they don't kick about it.

Not at the price they are
getting.

Yes, they are content with
the price.

They get more than the
people in Ontario.

And so they should. How
many householders have you? Have you anything like 651?
Here they get only $38.
Produce the figures.

Speaking to the resolution
I asked the minister to tell us on what basis he was paying this war-time bonus. I have

Postal Service
been listening intently ever since, but the nearest I could get to an answer was the minister's statement last night that some of these men come in and ask for small amounts. If they ask for small amounts, they get small amounts.

No, they get
the small amount if in order to carry their contract with success they require it. We do not give a small amount simply because a man asks for it. He gets it only if it is justified.

I am just repeating the
minister's words. I listened to the explanation given to the hon. member for Peterborough West. In this connection I should like to place on record three specific cases, all running out of the same post office, and numbered as routes one, two and three. There is only about half a mile difference in the distance of these three routes, and a difference of only five m the number of boxes served by the three.
The price for the first of these is $385 a year, six trips per week. This man asked for a war-time bonus, and was given one of $100. That brings his price today up to $485, or $34.40 per mile. The man running on the next route had a contract price of S482 and, upon request, received a bonus of $118.

What is the
mileage?

The mileage varies only
half a mile in these three routes, and there is a difference of only five in the number of boxes.

We would
not be able to give an answer unless we had the number of the route, and the post office.

I can give it. How does
the department arrive at the amount of the war-time bonus? The $118 paid to the last mentioned man gave him a total cheque of $600 per year, or $41.38 per mile. The third man-and this is the route which is a half mile longer than the other two-is operating on a tender of $324. Upon request he was given a bonus of $116.20, bringing him to a total of $440.20 per year, or a mileage rate of $29.34.
These three routes are almost identical in distance, and all run out of the same post office. They cover the same kind of roads, and as I have pointed out there is a variation of only five in the number of boxes. Yet the mileage rate varies from $29.34 to $41.38.
What is the name of the distributing office?
I shall give that to the minister later.
I can answer only generally, because I would have to go into the details and look at the files. We cannot have these details in the memoranda before us.

Before the minister answers let me assure him that I am not finding fault, nor am I criticizing those who are receiving bonuses. What I am trying to find out is how t'he minister's department arrives at the bonus given to these men.

I am sure that in these cases the amounts granted were those asked. There was a difference in the initial price, and that initial price was not fixed by the post office department, but rather by the gentlemen who tendered. When a bonus was asked we had only one thought in mind, and that was to give a bonus which was not more than it should have been. If a contractor asked for a bonus of $118 over and above what he was receiving, and if we found that that amount was reasonable for him, we would give him the $118, but we would not tell him that we could give him $216. Because, after all, we have to be careful with the taxpayers' money. The initial price is not fixed by us; it is fixed by the contractor who gets the contract because he has tendered at a certain price.

It all reverts to what I said at the beginning. If these men bid a small amount, they get a small amount. The minister has mentioned' t'he initial contract and I should like to ask him this:	When a
rural mail route is put up for tender and several tenders come in. why is it that occasionally a tender is not accepted but the route is put up again? I know the minister will say that that is done because the department feels the tenders were too high, but I know of one case where there was a difference of only $55. The carrier who had been doing the job for several years tendered at the same rate he was getting, including the bonus, and the contract was sent back the second time for tenders and was finally given to another man who tendered a few dollars less. That man was given to understand by the person who 'had the patronage for the constituency that he would receive the war-time bonus.

Nobody had any authority to do that, and I must tell the hon. gentleman that no bonus has been given
Postal Service

unless the contract has been in effect for nearly a year. I cannot give an answer now to his question about the calling of new tenders, but if the hon. gentleman will give me t'he name I shall have t'he files looked up and give him a reply.

I can give the minister the reason. It was done because the department felt that there were not enough people who knew about it when it was put up for tender. The strange thing is that there were three tenders the first time and three tenders the second time. In my opinion it all simmers down to this:	There is a great deal of discriminatory action in paying these fees. No doubt the men are given exactly what they ask for, but I do not think it is fair for any department of government to take an attitude that one man will be paid $29 per mile while another man is paid $42 per mile driving over the same roads, the difference being made up by the war-time bonus. If they go in and tender and there is no bonus, then I have no argument. If the government is trying to satisfy these people, I do not think they are doing a very good job of it when they permit such discriminations as I have described. It would seem to be a horse-trading policy where you are trying to get all you can for the least possible amount of money, and if John Jones will do the work all right.

It is not the least possible amount of money; it is a reasonable amount of money. I admit that with all these rural mail contracts there are many requests for this and that. We try to be fair.
I should not be surprised if on looking through 14,000 mail contracts you found here and there things that should have been done another way. I admit that this may happen as long as we cannot have a yardstick which would be applicable. Certain contracts must be given under the tender system. This system is acceptable by all governments as being the best way of granting contracts. Otherwise we would again have the patronage flag, if you want to call it that, which would, be much worse.
We should have some yardstick for the war-time bonus.

An effort to obtain it has been made, not only by the Liberal government but by the Conservative government. A few years ago a gentleman by the name of MacKinnon tried to form an organization of rural mail contractors. He lobbied hon. members under the Borden and Meighen governments and under the Liberal 
government. Efforts have been made to find a yardstick for these contracts. We are granting a bonus in the Post Office Department for the best design for new stamps, and we will gladly pay one for a yardstick system which would be above criticism. It would be grand if the department could have one, but up to this time I do not know of any; neither do my officials.

Mr. Chairman, I suggest that you ask the minister to come down to one of these vacant seats in the centre of the chamber where we can hear this whispering campaign that is going on at the Speaker's end of the chamber.

The Postmaster General has referred to the difficulty of obtaining a proper yardstick, but it seems to me that the department has some sort of yardstick to decide whether tenders are too high. We know of cases where all the tenders have been refused and the contracts advertised again. Then they also seem to have a yardstick by which they decide that a rural mail service *will be given only when there are so many people per mile. In view of those two instances I think the minister diould go back to his department and have them make a more valiant attempt to get a proper yardstick for the granting of these bonuses as well as for the acceptance of tenders for mail contracts.
I think all of us realize that the situation in connection with the tender system is an unfortunate one, both to the people served bv the rural mail service and to some of the rural mail carriers. I do not think this problem is impossible of solution. As the hon. member for New Westminster has said, mileage is not the only thing to be considered, nor is the number of people per mile. Climatic and road conditions and other factors enter into the picture. If rural mail carriers have been foolish enough, if you want to use that language, to tender on a contract at a price below that at which they can give economic service and because of which they are sacrificing their own interests as well as the interests of the people they serve, then I think we should make a more determined effort to cure this situation and provide a better postal service.
In dealing with this matter of rural mail delivery we have to realize that the people being served are suffering when there is poor mail service. We do not feel that the tender system is conducive to a good and efficient rural mail service. This is the second year after the war, and the minister tells us he is going to continue the bonus policy for another

Postal Service
year. We know also that rural mail carriers who have submitted tenders within the last three or four years will have an opportunity to revise their tenders within the next one or two years. Therefore there is no need to have this bonus at this particular time. If a rural mail carrier has made too low a tender, in a very short time he will have the opportunity of making a new tender and curing his uneconomic position. If the tender system is to be adhered to I see very little to be gained by continuing the power of the minister to grant bonuses, because he has not used it during the past year. If we do not continue the tender system we should get a better one. It simply resolves itself into that-
Will the hon. member permit a question? What suggestion has he to make?
I shall answer that very quickly. Put this party in power and you will have it solved.
Come over and give us a hand.

I had not intended taking part in this discussion but I think so much of the plight of the rural mail carriers that I say God help them if they have to wait until the other party gets into power to get any help from that quarter.

The granting of these wide powers to the minister is a subject he does not like to hear about, but as I see the situation we are going to place in his possession a great big patronage melon which he will be able to slice up in whatever way he sees fit and distribute without any right of control by parliament. In an effort to find out just how large this melon will be I should like to ask the minister a simple question. To how many contracts will the power apply? In how many cases will he have the power to grant supplementary allowances outside of contracts where there are bonuses? Can he give us a list by provinces or by postal districts across Canada of the number of contracts in respect of which he would have the power to grant supplementary allowances? That is a simple question, and it will start something.
It would be impossible to answer the question exactly.
Within one hundred contracts.

We have
already given bonuses to 4,000 contracts. On at least 1,500 or 2,000 contracts we would
not need to give bonuses, and I would not be able to give any because they have not yet run for a year; the law would not allow me to give a bonus in these cases. There may be people who could apply, and some would have a chance of obtaining a bonus, but others would surely not, because I must tell the hon. member that quite a large number have been refused bonuses.
At the moment I am not interested in the number who have been refused; I am interested in the number who have qualified.

The 4,000 who received their contracts through tenders did not ask for a bonus. They could not ask because they received their contracts at a time when they should have known about the high cost of living.

That is a fine
answer, but it does not give any particulars. We are back to this, that in general figures, even on the minister's own statement, he is going to be able to play around with the awarding of supplementary payments in some six thousand contracts.
Eight thousand.
It is 8,500.

I was understating it, sir. There are approximately 8,500 contracts under which parliament is to empower the minister, in his discretion and without control, to award these bonuses, which I see run from $140 to $275, $360, $200, and so on.
And $50 and $30.
There are not very many of these. I have a list in my hand from one constituency which shows that there were five awards, and of these five the smallest was $140, except for one at $50.
Does the hon. member object to that?

There is one for $140 and others for $275, $200 and $360. That indicates, sir, the danger of the procedure that we are asked to approve. It gives the minister the right to expend a great deal more than I had thought we were being asked. It will run as high as $800,000, or certainly not far removed from that amount, which will be in the control of the minister to dispense with whatever bounty he chooses. I cannot understand why we cannot get the records province by province.

You will
get it.
Postal Service
When?
We cannot give it today, but I told the hon. member that we could answer any question and give the total with details of all the bonuses which have been given.

There is nothing in the public accounts dealing with these bonuses. Nobody knows who got them, when they were awarded, or the amounts. I have gone through the records of the public accounts for 1945-46, and if the minister can point out where these records are shown I shall be glad to have the information.
According to the estimate I made the other night the minister has so far awarded approximately $800,000 at his own discretion under the order in council. If one thing more than another is necessary to ensure care in expenditures by the ministers it is publicity as to the amounts and particulars. I repeat that nowhere in the public accounts is there anything to indicate what awards have been made, in what provinces, or the particulars of the awards. I ask the minister to furnish the committee with these records. We should like a record of the number of contracts, province by province, or by postal districts, to which bonuses have been granted, the total amounts of such bonuses in each year since 1944, and the date.
The minister would lead the committee to believe that he has been extremely careful in awarding supplementary bonuses. He says he has turned them down in some cases. Will he give the committee the numbers which have been turned down?-because that is contrary to what he told us last night.

Not at all. I am sorry, it is not contrary to what I said before. When we were discussing the question yesterday we were talking about the contracts where bonuses wrere granted, not the contracts where they were not granted.

As I understood the minister last night the principle followed was, to him who asks shall be granted. I believe that epitomizes the method of awarding these supplementary grants. If a man did not ask for a bonus he did not get it.
That is not what hon. members sitting around the hon. gentleman understood, because most of them claimed that we were parsimonious in handing out bonuses.

We are not talking now about the question of parsimony. All of us agree to the necessity of war bonuses being granted, but we are anxious to know that the

minister shall not have the control over several hundreds of thousands of dollars to spend as he pleases, to dispose of as he sees fit, to award to friends whom he picks out for his beneficence, at the expense of the people of Canada. That is what we object to, and that is why we ask for information, full and detailed, in regard to the matter.
When this bill is passed will it empower the minister to grant bonuses or supplementary awards under air mail contracts? I am quite interested in asking that, because originally it started out as an award for the mail carriers.
I may say at once that these mail contracts are awarded in virtue of order in council. There is an order in council for every one of them.
Does the minister say this applies only to contracts that are let by tender?
Yes, let by tender-all mail contracts let by tender. Of course, mail contracts under $200 do not come under this.

This measure doe3 not grant power to the minister to increase the amount of any air mail contracts with any of the air companies who are today engaged in the carrying of mail. That is perfectly clear?
Yes, it is.

Before we go further. I wonder if we could get a general statement of the amount of bonuses paid each year, the number of applicants who apply, and the numbers turned down, so that we shall have a full understanding of the power the minister is asking for. Surely the house is not to be asked to confer a power like this when the minister cannot himself tell the house how extensive that power will be, or the amount of money which is to be put in his hand for expenditure.

I have to disagree with the
member for Lake Centre, because I cannot exactly blame the minister for everything that has happened. My experience has been that it is the inspector in the area in which we live. In my particular case, it is the inspector in Calgary. Any correspondence that I have had wth the Postmaster General has always been referred to the inspector in Calgary. I have sometimes thought that if we could get by that inspector we might get somewhere, but it is impossible to get by him. I often wish we could take matters up with the Postmaster General, instead of having to go to the inspector. I know that

Postal Service
in my area there are many who have mail contracts and I am sure they have been unaware of any bonus being paid by the department which the Postmaster General administers. If they had known of that bonus I am sure they would have made application.
1 want to be able to hear what the Postmaster General says in the house or in committee. To those of us who are sitting in this corner the debate sounds like a private conversation between the minister and members directly opposite. I agree with the member for Selkirk that the minister should move up a few seats so as to enable us all to hear him. I do not like to sit here all the time and hear nothing that is going on. I want to know what the minister is saying because we in this corner are just as much entitled to hear what is going on as anyone else, but we do not know what is going on when we sit here and hear nothing but a murmur between the Postmaster General and the members directly across from him. I suggest very earnestly that he move up a few seats so that we can all hear him.

What our rural mail carriers need and what they want is security and a living wage, and I do not think that any man who has been carrying the mails for over ten or twelve years should have to submit a tender in order to obtain security. I do not think that a postman or a postmistress who has been in office for ten years should be required to submit a tender. In my opinion it is not fair. However, I pay my tribute to the officials of the department who are always willing to listen to what members have to say about their own constituencies. My representations have been properly received, but I have always rebelled against the idea that a man who has been carrying mail for ten years or more should be required to submit a tender. I know one man in my constituency who has a right to security because he has a wife and twelve children, not born in the province of Quebec either. I say that man should be secure and should not have to submit a tender.

I think there should be
some new and better method, in a public utility such as the post office, of fixing the actual out of pocket expenses of those affected by this bill. No large department store would conduct its bonus business in this way. The post office is a great public utility for which the people have considerable respect, but the conditions rural, urban and suburban of its rank and file have not been what they should be. I would point out to the minister what I regard as a defect in this method of doing
business from the commercial aspect, but before I do so I wish to compliment him in one respect. We are considering this matter on the sixteenth and seventeenth days of the session whereas last year it was brought up on August 6, the ninety-sixth day of the session. So the minister has made some progress in that direction.
We all realize that the cost of living has gone up, the cost of cars, gasoline, tires, parts, labour, and so on, but I suggest that the British postal service would not conduct their business in this way. What is being done? You have a surplus in the Post Office department, and a very large one, because according to the records there were receipts last year of $68 million odd and expenditures amounting to roughly $57 million. There was a surplus of some $10,905,000 for the last year of record. In 1945, the year before, there was a surplus of $11,442,503; in 1944, $12,585,910. What I am complaining about is that the department, instead of having taken this out of the war bonus, is starving some of the other services in order to pay this bonus to some. Only about fifty per cent are getting it; the other fifty per cent do not. In the first place, as this is a great, useful public utility, it is the desire of the taxpayers who contribute to the post office that they should have the benefit of these useful services at cost. But this is not being done in connection with this work.
Take the post office in Toronto, for example. It contributes $13,807,000 a year, whereas the Montreal post office contributes only $10,321,000. There is a surplus in favour of Toronto over Montreal of $3,500,000. What are you doing to pay this supplementary bonus for the rural mail delivery where it is no doubt badly needed? You have no system run from the commercial aspect. You are starving the city service for it. Business districts that are contributing $11,600,000 are cut down to one delivery a day. In war and since, residential districts were cut down to one delivery a day, and postmen had to cover two or three times the area. That should not be necessary. If you want to run this department on a commercial basis, well and good; pay the proper war bonus to all on the basis of out of pocket expenses.
Some of these people are on contract and some are not on contract. Some of the contracts have elapsed and some of the contractors do not want to carry on. There should not be a system of robbing Peter to pay Paul, taking the large surplus of three and a half million contributed by our city and starving for it the other services. We should long ago have had a revision of the whole schedule of supplementary rates. Let us have
Postal Service

a business administration in the department. 1 know it is a hard thing to handle. They are continuing now a five per cent bonus, and in some cases at a rate of $50 a mile. With improved roads, and deliveries in the suburban districts like summer resort districts and that kind of thing, there should be some other way of handling out these supplemental appropriations to pay all, not just some of these mail contracts.
We hope, Mr. Chairman, that the various departmental officials who are travelling around a good deal and the ministers who travel abroad will come back with some new ideas in relation to this question. Some further investigation of it should be made, because the present post office system is carrying only about fifty per cent of the functions, rural, urban and suburban, carried by the British post office. We should have some further investigation in connection with this work.
Every rural mail deliverer, whether or not he has a contract, should have been notified of this particular act. An advertisement in the Canada Gazette is not enough. He should also have a chance to file a return or a report showing what his actual out of pocket expenses were from the commercial aspect. Every department store has the same trouble as the post office has had herein in connection with increased costs in war, and, after it, increased costs of supplies, labour and equipment. In the construction of the. Queen Elizabeth highway, such rural postal services on the Dundas highway and Queen street you now pass are in some cases obsolete. What I should like to see the minister do is this.
I am quite in favour of paying them' all a fair, just rate as a public utility, a public utility which has all along had impossible labour conditions. I wish to see some of the labour conditions which I have seen in the Toronto post office and others throughout the country greatly improved. They are intolerable labour conditions for people working in a utility which reaches every home in Canada, and relates to every retail man and wholesale man.
On the efficiency of the post office depend the trade and commerce of this country. During the recess of the house, we should make some further investigation into this supplementary bonus. I should like to see it carried on in the way it is done in the United States. I believe we can learn a great deal over there. We can also learn a great deal in rural administration from the British post office. Surely the surplus, which is getting larger all the time, should be handed back to the consumer in lessened cost and to labour, or some of it at least to the men, women and

children working in the various branches of the post office. I have seen some of these contracts. I have received a great many letters from all over Canada about the rural mail delivery. The minister should notify all these people that they may get actual out of pocket expenses, whether they have a contract or whether it has expired. It should be automatic and include all.
In my opinion, this is one department where there is more politics than in any other department I ever saw in my life. I visited some post offices and saw the difficulty returned soldiers have in getting on at Christmas time on temporary work and other things like that which have been going on for some years. I have yet to see any improvement made in the case of the returned men who are coming home. I believe the country would support the government in having a proper method, from the commercial aspect, of handing out these bonuses for the actual out of pocket expenses. Whether Grit, Tory or C.C.F., the people have rights as citizens of the country. No other public utility could handle labour in this way. A great public utility such as a light, heat and power utility could not do it. There woud be a strike if they conducted proceedings in the way adopted by the post office, with patronage and all that kind of thing in connection with it.
I do not say that the present government is any worse than preceding ones. I have been complaining about the low pay and labour conditions in the post office for many years. There should be some different system in a great, national public utility such as this, one similar to the system adopted by other large public utilities in this country where they improve the lot of the workers, sub-officials, give them larger pay, better working conditions, pensions, five days a week for some of them, holidays of two weeks and all that kind of thing. I should like to see that principle carried into the post office for the sake of the hardworking people, rural, urban and suburban, in it. While I sympathize with the minister in what he is doing, I believe there should be some improvement made by giving all their actual out of pocket expenses, from the commercial aspect.

I am not going to discuss
the merits or demerits of the tender system at any great length, other than to say that being a practical man, and having been brought up in a rural constituency, I cannot see any other practical alternative at the present time. Some hon. members have spoken of standardization of equipment. I do not see how you can standardize equip-

Postal Service
ment any more than you can standardize the different types of clothes men wear to perform different jobs, because you have to have a vehicle or the other type of equipment that you are to use to do the job. You may have to go over rough roads. You may have to go over paved roads. Aou may have to use a dog sleigh. You may have to use a boat. How are you to standardize your equipment? I maintain that the tender system as it now exists is the only practical system we can employ at the present time.
The main thing we are considering in this bill is supplemental payments on mail contracts. I must confess that I was worried some months ago as to what would happen, after the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act expired, regarding the bonuses that had been paid as a war-time measure; and I was very happy when I saw this bill introduced because I know it is necessary. We must all realize that it is merely an expedient to take care of a temporary situation. I think if we looked that fact in the face we should not have such great worries regarding entrusting the minister with a few hundred thousand dollars which he may need to tide us over in these times. After all, ministers are responsible for much larger sums than that, and I cannot see the great danger that we are worrying about.
This bill is obviously just an expedient. Many of these rural mail carriers need the supplement. They are not interested in how many words we put on Hansard; they are interested in getting money, and so I say, let us get on with the bill.

I am going to obey the instructions I got from the last speaker and get on with the bill. It seems to me that everyone in this house is agreed on one thing and that is that our postal service employees working on a regular job are not properly paid. What we are quarreling about, it seems to me, is largely a matter of method.
I have a letter from the secretary of the rural mail couriers' association. I am not suggesting that I am very important on that account because I am sure that all hon. members got the same letter. They are suggesting a mileage basis, and they say that ninety-nine per cent of the replies they have had from Vancouver to Halifax are in favour of that basis. They appreciate the difficulties that would arise on the odd route but they think something might be done to overcome that.
I hope I understood the minister correctly, that this is a temporary measure. May we
infer from what he has said that there is to be a general revision of this whole rate structure?	_
I am going to give the committee something else which came to my attention just before I came down here. In the Post Office Department and in the Department of Mines and Resources-and I am sure it applies to all the departments-if an employee is dismissed foi misconduct not only does he lose all his pension rights but he loses his own money which he has paid in to the government during all his service. The hon. member for Broadview said a moment ago that the treatment of labour in this utility, as he calls the postal service, was not to our credit. The man I speak of has paid over two thousand dollars of his own money into the government pension fund. He stole $3 and was dismissed. I was very close to the defence, and the situation was this. After all this length of service, and service in two wars, this man took three SI bills which were placed in decoy letters and addressed to a radio preacher broadcast. As a matter of fact, if anybody wants to get really rich in this world, the best way I know of doing it is to secure a broadcast hour and to go into that business, because it is the most lucrative I know of, as Father Coughlin and Gerald Smith have proven. These letters were decoys addressed to a particular religious broadcast called the "Sunrise Gospel Hour''
We shall never hear it then.

An hon. member suggests that that is too early for him, but may I say that it is never too late for a sinner who repents. I mention this case to the Postmaster General and to the committee for this reason. I am in entire agreement with what the hon. member for Broadview said as to the rigidity, the stinginess, if you like, with which we treat not only our postmen but our whole public service. Someone may say that there are many applicants for civil service jobs. There are. They want these jobs why? Because, while they will have to work for less than they might earn elsewhere, they are told that there is security at the end of the road. Security? Well, bread and butter-that is all there is at the end of the road. But people who are capable of earning more money elsewhere take these positions through fear, through the desire for security.
I accept, by implication if necessary, the statement made by the Postmaster General last evening that he has in mind a complete revamping of this whole position. It is not good enough just to say that the tender method which we now use, where a couple of
Postal Service

neighbours are competing against one another, should not be up for renewal year after year; I trust that there will be a complete review of the whole position. So I leave the letter of the rural mail couriers' association before the Postmaster General. I also suggest that not only in this department but in all other departments we eliminate this rule whereby a man who is dismissed for misconduct, even though it be his first mistake in twenty-five years of service, loses not only the pension benefits he would have got from the government but also his own money which he has paid in on a percentage salary deduction basis to the government. I am sorry that the Minister of Mines and Resources is not here at the moment because he knows of a similar case that I took up with him, in which complete restitution was made and yet the man comes out a convict and with not a thing to go on with, although this government has several thousand dollars of his money.

I agree with many hon. members that there is room for improvement in the Post Office Department. I live in an urban and rural constituency, and I hold in my hand a list of places where there is plenty of room for improvement, and much improvement. I will speak first of the post office in the town in which I live, Beausejour, Manitoba. The postmaster there gets $210 a year and the revenue from that post office is over $7,000 a year. He has to keep his car in a garage at a cost of seventy-five cents a day, so that he is more or less out of pocket. He has complained to me several times. The contract has been advertised twice, but there have been no other applicants because this postmaster has held the position for practically twenty-five years and the people of the town think he has done a good job. His services have been satisfactory and he is entitled to fair pay. Surely we are not going to ask government employees to render service for nothing. We do not want them to put in their time for nothing.
I agree with some hon. gentlemen who have suggested that we should set up a yardstick by which the value of the service they render could be measured. It has been pointed out this afternoon that the routes vary widely, that on two routes covering the same distance, one man serves 600 houses and another man eleven. I do not think it would be an impossible task for a committee to map out the various routes and set rates which would be equitable all along the line.
I, too, have a bone to pick with the Postmaster General about war bonuses. I wrote the Post Office Department, stating that, if a

man were entitled to a bonus in one place, he should be entitled to it in the other. But in the way it has been carried out, the wheel that squeaked the most got the most grease. That should not be so.
There are many mail contractors who carried out their service faithfully, but who did not get the bonus, simply because they had too much pride to ask for more money, although they were entitled to it, just the same as the man who had the gall to ask for it. If we are to help these mail contractors we must set a fair schedule all the way through. Treat them all alike; give them a fair day's pay for a fair day's work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I remind the committee that we are considering Bill No. 17, respecting supplemental payments on mail contracts. The debate at this stage should not be on the administration of the post office, generally, or on postal employees, but should be strictly relevant to the bill. In fact, in my opinion it should be relevant only to the section under consideration.
I am not going to be too strict in this respect because, when I suggested last night that we should discuss the sections as they are called, it was decided by the committee that there should be more latitude allowed in the discussion. At this time, however, I must remind the committee that we are dealing with supplemental payments on mail contracts.

Was consideration given to giving increases to rural mail carriers on the same basis as that used in connection with the cost of living bonus? I believe hon. members will agree that, if discretionary powers had been left to each cabinet minister to decide just how much should be given to each individual employee, the provisions with respect to cost of living bonus would have brought about a chaotic state of affairs in the past few years. If a rural mail contractor takes a contract to deliver mail for so much a year and then, through no fault of his own, prices of gasoline and tires go up by ten or fifteen per cent, he has a legitimate claim to accept additional compensation.
Could the Postmaster General give us some indication as to how much it would cost to have a straight percentage increase right across the board, and if even at this stage he might agree to introduce this principle for the remainder of the period, as was suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre? I understood the hon. member to say that about 14,000 contracts are involved, of which bonuses have been given to something over 4,000, and that 3,000 or 4,000 are not eligible because of

Postal Service
the recent date of their contracts. But we have about 7.000 disgruntled persons in Canada who have a legitimate grievance.
They are not all disgruntled.

They will be after they read this debate. I think everyone in that category will have a real grievance. Did the Postmaster General or his department consider giving the bonus to everyone, and would he give the committee an estimate as to how much it would cost if the grant were made on a cost of living basis to everyone involved?

It would be impossible to arrive at that calculation at this time, and also impossible of application. These contracts are being renewed. A considerable number are renewed each month, and tenders are still being called in some cases. For instance, if a contractor dies, we must ask for tenders, and when those tenders are filed they are filed in the light of living conditions today. The tenderer knows the cost of gasoline and tires at this time; he knows what it will cost to buy an automobile and will calculate his tender accordingly.
Mr. BRADSHAW; What is the largest amount of bonus that has been paid in any one instance?
I promised the hon. member for Lake Centre that I would file a document showing the details in respect of all bonuses. If there are reasons set out in the files, we shall give those reasons.
I am not opposing the bill, but I know of an instance in my own constituency where a bonus of $400 is being paid on a contract of $600. That seems out of proportion.
If the hon. member wants to give us the circumstances and the number of the contract we shall give him the reason.
We want the information from the minister.
How can any minister have all that information in his mind concerning 14,000 contracts?

That is exactly the position here. The minister comes and asks for a blanket authority to spend more than $800,000. We ask him for details, and he tells us he has not those details but that he will bring them next Monday, or some time next week when the committee has ceased to sit. He has an official before him now, but no
documents in regard to this matter. I say we have a right to this information, and until we get it we are in no position to decide one way or another as to the merits of one part of the bill.
Surely the minister does not come here and say, "If you know of a case where we allowed a bonus of $400 on a $600 contract, tell us about it, and we will answer it." Surely he will not say that, when the simple question asked by the hon. member was as to the amount of the largest bonus. To that question the answer given by a responsible minister is, "I don't know; do you think I would have that information?" Surely he has some records.
I have information, but I do not have it in my mind.
And the minister does not appear to have it anywhere else, and does not want to produce it. That seems to be the attitude. We asked for it last night.
Shame.

Oh, that, type of interruption does not bother me at all. But it does show that I am dealing with something which some hon. members believe should not be brought to the attention of the committee. That is why they take the attitude they do. All we want is information, but the only information we get from the minister is a lengthy disquisition in respect of generalities, instead of answers to the questions asked. We want to know now, from him, about this power which is placed in him.
I come back to the public accounts for 1946, and I find in them not one suggestion of any such payments being made. It sets out these:
Mail Service by Ordinary Land Conveyance, Including Rural Mail Delivery
Estimates	 $9,050,000
Allotments	 8,903,500
Expenditures	 8,904,984
Not a word is mentioned about the amount of awards given by the minister under an order in council passed pursuant to the War Measures Act. Then on the next page, Q-16, is set forth the amounts expended in each of the districts for rural mail routes, side services, stage services and city services. But there is not a word to indicate the amount of the original contracts, or how much was added by way of bonus or supplementary grant. It is simply general information on which no one can come to any conclusion. Yet last night when I said that this was placing tremendous pow'er in the minister's hands, he said I was overstating the case.
Postal Service

The minister says that today there are about 8,000 contracts that he will be able to play around with. If this is to be an election year we know' the sort of playing around that will be done with the money of the Canadian people if it is left under the control of the minister, and that is why we want the information.
Every one of us is in favour of the bonus; we did not vote against the principle of the bill, but we want information as to what is to be done with the money being handed to the minister in the form of a blank cheque. Past experience has not shown that the minister has always acted in. accordance with propriety in the matter of recommendations. I suggest that we are entitled to this information. We are going to have this information; the minister can simply get in touch with his department and let us have it and then it will be all over. But he adopts the attitude of postponement and procrastination; he says that next week, next Monday, next Tuesday or some other day he will be in position to lay the information on the table of the house. He should give it to us now and then we can get through with this matter.
I would gladly give it to the hon. gentleman, but it would be impossible to pick one contract out of so many.
That is true.
I am sorry I cannot do it because I should like to do it.
I did not ask for any particular contract; I asked for the highest bonus that has been paid.

In order to give that information, I would have to go through the contracts. The hon. member mentioned $400 and I am sure there are some contracts where that amount has been paid. If he is talking about $1,000 I do not think there are any as high as that, with the exception of certain city services where fleets of trucks are involved, and I am not sure of the particular ones.

There are probably as many rural mail routes in my constituency as anywhere else in the country. I consider it most unfair that certain rural mail carriers have been paid bonuses, wrhile others who did not know that a bonus was available have not received anything. I think that is one of the great instances of unfairness in connection with this matter. It seems to me that the government, of all organizations, should pay for services rendered.

I agree with the hon. member for Lake Centre when he says that there should be some basis upon which this bonus is paid. It does not seem to me to be good business simply to permit the Postmaster General to pay out money to these rural mail carriers without there being some basis of payment. The information we have asked for is germane and I do not think our request should be ignored by the minister. Information given after the bill is passed will be of no use to us in considering the bill.
When a mail route is lengthened, that is, where a man has bid on a route of ten or fifteen miles and later on the route is extended, is that extension paid for on a mileage basis, or is a new tender asked for?
It is on a pro rata basis.

During the war many applications were made in my constituency either for the extension of rural mail routes or for the setting up of new routes. The answer was always that this could not be done during the war. According to the hon. member for Lake Centre, it is proposed to pay out something like $800,000 in bonuses. Is it the policy of the government to extend present rural mail routes and set up new ones? The argument before w'as that there was not suflicient money.

During the war we were not short of money because we spent quite a lot, but we were short of equipment and man-power. At the present time we are extending mail routes but, in doing so, we follow a certain rule. For example, there must be four households in every mile of the proposed extension. There may be a route of five miles and new houses have been built along another two miles of the route. If there are eight households in those two miles we would extend the route, even though it was necessary for the mail carrier to retrace his route.

Are changes in routes made on the recommendation of the inspector or on requests being received from the people in the district? I have in mind, a case where a change is being made to which the people are opposed. I believe the inspector has recommended it and the department is carrying it out.
It is generally done at the request of the people. At other times new routes are offered to the people, in which cases they have to buy the standard boxes and instal them.

I do not want the committee to be misled by the statement I made

Postal Service
a little while ago as to the postmaster getting $210. That was not his total remuneration; that was what he receives for carrying mail from the station to the post office. His contract was for $200 and he received an operational bonus of $10. which totaled $210. He does not receive any war-time bonus. He must keep his car in a garage in order to meet the train both night and morning. Sometimes there are as many as ten or fifteen heavy bags of mail, and during the rush times I have seen him make two or three trips. I should like to have the Postmaster General adjust this matter as soon as possible.

I want it to be quite clear that I am not against the principle of this bill; it is just the manner in which these bonuses are paid. I understand t'he difficulties with which the Postmaster General is faced. He said yesterday that the operational bonus of five per cent was paid on all routes. In our own case he said it was not true.
I said that the first bonus given in 1941 was a five per cent increase; it was an increase on the general cost.
It was not paid to all contract holders.

Yes, it was. I said that it was paid on all contracts, the rates of which were determined on or before the 21st day of April, 1941. April 21 was the date on which there was an increase in the price of gasoline; therefore we could not pay in cases where the rate was determined after that date.

I will accept that. I note that the war-time bonus ranges all the way from 124 per cent to 100 per cent; that is giving the mileage rate anywhere from thirty-six miles to a high of fifty-four miles. I agree with the fact that probably some of the routes could be handled and more money saved actually on the thirty-six mile basis than on other routes of a fifty-four mile basis. I understand that. The hon. member for New Westminster said that on one of his routes there were 651 box holders. I should like to suggest to the Postmaster General that, if he would permit some of these boxes to be placed at one stop, it would allow for the servicing of three or four boxes at one time at one stop, which would make it easier to handle the route.
They do that.
That is good. In our districts they will not allow them to do it.
There are as many as ten at some corners.
Does the hon. gentleman say that we do not allow people along the route to group their boxes together?
Not close enough near one stop to permit the courier to handle two boxes at the one time.

If a man is satisfied to put his box at the door of a neighbour where the contractor may serve it in one movement, deposit the mail in these two boxes at the same time, we have no objection at all. The contrary is rather the truth. When some farmers are living on a small route where the contractor would have to retrace his route in order to come back on the main road we ask them to put their boxes together and sometimes we have difficulty to get them to agree. .

As I said before, it probably would be much easier for a man to handle a route of ten or twelve miles with 651 box holders than it would be to handle a route of thirty-five miles with only eleven box holders. Will the hon. member for New Westminster state the number of miles on the route to which he refers? It is also possible that a route of only eleven miles with 651 box holders may be worth no more money than a route of thirty-five miles with eleven box holders, depending on the road conditions.
I should like to know the basis upon which these bonuses were given, because in some cases where a man has received only $36 a mile he has not received a bonus; in other cases where a man gets $54 a mile he has not received a bonus, but in still other cases where the mileage rate received is over $45 or $50 he has received a bonus. I do not understand why a yardstick could not be found. There is nothing impossible in it if you go about it in the right way. Why would it not be possible to adopt the suggestion in the letter of the rural mail carriers which I suppose every hon. member received, and which suggested that some $50 a mile basis be used. Would it not be possible to arrive at some basis along that line without giving the Postmaster General a blank cheque? Generally we limit the amount of money that can be spent in that way. Why would it not be possible to limit the bonus and bring all the contracts up to the basis of $50 a mile on all mail contracts signed before January 1, 1947? There would be no point in giving a bonus to * man who signed
Postal Service

a contract since that date. It should be possible to arrive at a figure on that basis and put a limit on the powers that the minister would have.
I do not think it would be impossible to group several routes and make one man responsible for two routes. In the minister's statement this afternoon,*he said that the short routes demanded a higher mileage rate. That is quite true because the man on the short route would probably lose half a day. He could not make a living on that short route; he would need to have some other means of livelihood, and yet it would take him a large part of the day to handle the route. That only makes the position much stronger when I say that I do not see why it could not be arranged to have two routes out of one post office handled by one man. Set a rate on it and have the courier pass a civil service examination as the mail couriers in the urban districts do. Put him under the civil service commission. I do not see why that is not possible. I am not suggesting that it be done in all cases, but it is a matter that should be considered.
I wish to refer to the extension policy of the government. I am told by the Post Office Department that extensions cannot be made where there are fewer than two people in a half mile. Since I have been told that, I know of several cases where the mail courier is travelling nine-tenths of a mile, seven-tenths of a mile, six-tenths of a mile going from a place close to another man's route. When there are three box holders and five families trying to get their mail within one-third of a mile of a corner I do not see why they should be asked to walk one-third of a mile, when a man would go half a mile for two. To me it seems absurd. I know the department has rules and they must be lived up to. I know of other cases where the couriers are going in from the other end of the concession and doing two and a half miles when they could go one-third of a mile and take care of five people. Will the minister answer that question?

The first suggestion of a minimum of $50 a mile would amount to a tremendous sum. I explained yesterday or perhaps earlier this afternoon that routes are different when you take everything into consideration. If we had a minimum it would have to be not only a minimum which would be reasonable for the one who has the easiest of all the routes but also a minimum which would be acceptable to a large number of routes. Then we would have many tenders at the minimum amount because the tenderers would know thev could make
[Mr. Charlton. 1
a lot of money by having the average minimum, and the fear of patronage, as hon. members suggested, would be worse than it is today with the tender system.
As regards the merging of routes, we have done that in certain places and are considering doing it wherever possible, but it does not always give satisfaction to the patrons because some of them receive their mail after the others. If we had four routes, let us say, in a village somewhere, which would provide a full day's work, from the postal point of view it would be a good thing to have one man doing the job and to pay him as a civil servant. But there would be a good deal of difficulty because people at the north end of the village, let us say, might be the last to receive their mail and of course they would protest. However, we are looking into the situation to see if there are any places where mail can be delivered the year round by automobile, and we might come to this conclusion.
With regard to the half-mile extension, we have always counted these routes and calculated the service by households, including sometimes one family, sometimes two or three. But if there are three or four families in one house-

I did not say three or
four families in a house, but three boxholders and five families receiving mail in those boxes within a third of a mile from the corner.

We could
arrange to look into that.

I did not intend to enter into this discussion at all because, in my opinion, the Post Office Department has been doing a good job with a bad situation. They did a wonderful job during the war years handling mail in this country and keeping things going, and now our hon. friends across the way claim that the Postmaster General ought to be more generous and pay more money, while at the same time they grumble about the amount of money that is being spent and object to allowing the measure to go through. The hon. member for Lake Centre makes a great noise on that angle of the situation. Naturally the Postmaster General cannot do this work himself and I presume he does not pretend to. It must form part of the work of the officials in the department.

We want to see them all
treated fairly.

Very well. Now that the hon. member mentions that, I will discuss that aspect right now. Someone asked what was the highest amount that had been paid

Postal Service
anywhere. I at once recalled a case that came to my notice shortly after I got into office as member of parliament for Renfrew North in the early spring of 1937. This particular man had not had a chance to recover from the condition of desperate poverty into which he had got himself as a result of the government of my hon. friends who sit opposite. His situation was so desperate that he clamoured for a mail contract at the price of 8400. Well, he got it by tender and carried on for a time but under Liberal rule he became dissatisfied and he tendered again when his contract expired and got his contract raised to $600 and finally to $800, or double what he had received at first. When times became greatly improved he was still not satisfied with the $800 and wanted to quit the job. The Post Office Department is generous in that regard, is always willing to allow a man to quit, provided that he can find someone else to take over the contract. This man was able to get someone to take it over and the new contractor carried on for a time, but he, too, began to clamour for help and relief. According to the most recent information I have, he was offered an increase of $100, bringing the contract up to $900, and still he was grumbling. I do not know whether he accepted it.
What suggestion have my hon. friends to offer? It is difficult to keep men on these jobs, and here we have a solution proposed for one year to make it possible for the Post Office Department at least to try to keep the men at work and have the mail delivered. The department is asking for an extension of the privilege for one year, and in all the criticism that has been made I have not heard anyone suggest an alternative. If my hon. friends will not allow the measure to go through, what is their alternative? If the Post Office Department cannot be allowed to handle these cases as individual cases, as they arise, then what method would my hon. friends opposite suggest? As I see it, we have been getting along fairly well and the mail service has been kept going. I think we ought to pass this measure and get on with the work.

I really intended to speak on a section of the proposed bill, but I suggest part of my remarks can be made now so that I shall give two five-minute speeches instead of one ten-minute speech and perhaps the committee will enjoy that better. I always enjoy a five-minute speech myself. I am speaking now because of something the hon. member for Lake Centre said with regard to the secrecy that has surrounded all these war bonuses, because that is 83166-43
actually the name-war bonuses-as I found out a little while ago. That is the reason why a great many of the mail carriers did not make application in time, and what the last speaker has said proves that fact. There was one man in particular who got two or three increases, while some did not get any.

The hon. member misunderstood me. This man got an increase from S400 by tendering, and when 'his contract expired he was raised to $600. When that contract was completed, by tendering he got another raise to $800, and the man following him got $100 more.

Last night it was suggested that anyone who wished to have information in regard to these matters could find it in the Canada Gazette, that being a publication which nearly everyone reads. Well, this morning I looked through the Canada Gazette and I could not find any information in this regard. I looked through the index; I looked at the dates of the orders in council, but I could not find out anything in that way. I tried then to get the orders in council because we had their numbers. I have not yet got a copy of P.C. 8490. But that does not make very much difference because what that order provided was like a gift from Santa Claus, coming in free as it did after the last day of October, 1941, and was, I believe, general in its application. It was, as somebody has said, a five per cent bonus. After that, there were several other orders in council, and I happen to have them in my hand. I do not think they were ever printed1, because this is what they call a mimeographed form. P.C. 2311, after a great many "whereases" at the beginning, has at the bottom, one enacting clause. Incidentally, this is dated March 24, 1942. I think I mentioned that a prior one was dated October 31, 1941. After the "whereases" it said:
Therefore, His Excellency the governor general in council, is pleased to empower and doth hereby empower the Postmaster General to make temporary arrangements for the conveyance of His Majesty's mails when in his opinion no other course of action is possible or no more favourable arrangements could be made through the invitation of public tenders.
I made inquiries to find out how this order in council went out to the people. It was not in the Canada Gazette, but there is in the public library here a bound copy of these orders in council. With the help of the librarian, I went through them and could find order in council numbered-about No. 2000- and this order in council is No. 2311-and then there was a jump to No. 2400. There was nothing published. You could not find n even if you went to the book that was issued

Postal Service

containing orders in council. This order in council was not quite satisfactory to someone, and on the following July 7, 1942, following some more "whereases", there was another enacting clause. And here is where the auditor general comes in. I am surprised that the auditor general, who has made certain pungent remarks about other matters in his reports each year, has never in any one of his reports to parliament mentioned the fact that there was a war bonus for rural mail carriers. I went back to 1942 or 1943, and followed each yearly report to parliament. Never in one case was it mentioned, as the hon. member for Lake Centre has stated, in the public accounts. I only mention the fact because the auditor general apparently had interpreted order in council PC. 2311 of March 24, 1942, as limiting the actions of the Postmaster General under that order in council to contracts which had expired1 or were about to expire. Then this new P.C. 5833 goes on to say that, whether they have expired or not, they give him the power to include the cancellation of any such contract; and that is apparently what was done in the case to which the hon. member for Renfrew North just referred.
He saw it in the Gazette.

The order in council reads:
... it is hereby extended to include the cancellation of any such contract on the written request of the contractor, and the entering into of temporary arrangements at an equitable rate, any such temporary arrangements-
I want hon. members to watch this.
-to cover the period up to the termination of the War Measures Act-
And that, remember, is going to end on March 31 of this year.
-at which time public tenders would be invited to place the contract arrangements on a regular basis.
This also was not sufficient because it was necessary to have another order in council, P.C. 4960. It is a good thing the minister mentioned the numbers of these orders in council, because I do not think anyone else in -the world knew where to find them. It was for that reason I was able to get this mimeographed copy, which contains more "whereases."
How many this time?

There are six this time. The last "whereas" clause reads:
That, after careful study, it is considered that >t would be decidedly advantageous to classify

any increases granted under this authority as in the nature of war-time bonus, retain the original contracts in operation, and revert to the actual contract terms upon termination of the War Measures Act.
So that now we have something different. All these bonuses which have been given are to end on March 31. That is, they were only given and could only be given under the order in council until the termination of the War Measures Act. Then we come to the small enacting clause which reads:
Therefore, His Excellency the governor general in council, on the recommendation of the Postmaster General, is pleased to order and doth hereby order that wherever possible the contracts which have been dealt with or which may be dealt with be retained in full force and effect and that any increases granted under authority of said orders in council P.C. 2341 or P.C. 5833 be discontinued when the War Measures Act is rescinded.
I heard it said that there were about 7,500 of these contracts which were not renewed in some way by tender. All these contracts will expire on March 31 next. We do not get very much help, as I have said, from the public accounts, but we do find this; and remember, I am not opposed to the giving of some increase to these rural mail men; I am only opposed to the way in which it is being given and the manner in which the amount is to be arrived at.
In the fiscal year ended March 31, 1942, the rural mail men received compensation to the extent of $3,029,000; in 1943 the amount went up slightly to $3,187,000; 1944, $3,464,000. The bonus perhaps was working and very soon perhaps the war bonus was also. In 1945, the amount was $3,735,000 and, in 1946, $3,897,000

not a great deal of increase as compared with the increase for the whole Post Office Department in so far as it affects land and air, because air came into the picture about that time. So far as the increase to the rural mail men was concerned there was only a thirty per cent increase. For the carrying of the mails by land and air the total increase was seventy-two per cent. It went up from $11,000,000 to $19,000,000. But there are, of course, other people interested besides the rural mail carriers. There are these side services and the stage services. The increases in these were slightly more than those to the rural mail carriers.
Then in the same column, or under the same heading are the city services, which I do not understand. Perhaps the city services are the services mentioned by the hon. member for New Westminster, because certainly if there were on any mail route the number of people mentioned by him, they were in the very suburbs of the city. I can well imagine

Postal Service
