that to be the case because while I do not know the number of families that each carrier in the city of Toronto serves, I have had occasion to use the mails in this door-to-door householder delivery, so that some of the people would get some good) literature by reading my speeches. Quite often it is only a part of a mail route that was used, but I know that on at least one of them there were over four hundred households to which mail was delivered by the man who went off carrying the mail in his arms in Toronto. I know that around that city the population is so dense outside of the district where the mail carriers go from door to door, that in the adjacent rural routes, there may be seven hundred mail boxes. As the hon. member from Vancouver has said is the case in his city, there may be ten, twelve, fourteen or sixteen boxes at one place. This makes many suburban routes not very different from the routes which the city mail carrier covers.
I now wish to read something from the same author quoted by the hon. member for Lake Centre last night, because there has been a great deal of secrecy about the promulgation of these orders in council. The book is "The principles and practice of the system of control over parliamentary grants," by Durell. I would suggest that every member of the government read this book and find out what the proper constitutional usage is. The writer states on page 6:
This can only be achieved by the full publication of authentic accounts and the influence of public opinion, direct or indirect. Secrecy breeds prodigality, oppression, and, if not injustice, at least a sense of injustice. Publicity is the safeguard of popular liberties, and secures control over the accounts.
I suggest that every mail courier who did not know about the orders in council giving authority for a bonus must feel a sense of injustice because of the secrecy there was about it. On the same page the author says:
Real responsibility cannot be attached to the acts of the executive without publicity, and can only be ensured if, after the executive has performed its part, the way in which that part has been performed is ascertained by independent officers, and the result made known to parliament.
The value of the publicity of the accounts-
There was no publicity about this war bonus, -is in direct proportion to their completeness and detailed information. However valuable a summarized statement may be in affording prima facie evidence that the provision made by parliament has been followed, it cannot in itself furnish that full information which parliament is entitled to have and which alone will enable it to follow up the expenditure.
I reserve anything further I have to say until section 3 is reached.

It has come out in this discussion that there were about 14,000 mail contracts and that in 1941 or 1942 representations were made to the government by some of the contractors that they could not carry out their duties efficiently without some kind of bonus, and so the government passed an order in council giving authority to pay the bonus. The Minister of Labour apparently has been trying to promote harmonious labour relations in this country, and we find another department of government taking authority to pay a bonus to the rural mail drivers and yet not advising them that they were going to pay such a bonus. I cannot imagine any company deciding to give an increase to its employees and then hiding that fact so that only those who heard about it and came forward to claim the increase would get it. The government should set an example in good labour relations, and when they realized that more money should be paid to the rural mail drivers, was it not only right that they should have informed the rural mail drivers that a bonus was to be paid? Then pay the bonus to all alike. Apparently 4,000 of these rural mail drivers received the bonus. What about the other fellows who did not know about the bonus and did not get it? Is it too late to do anything for them? Are they just out of the picture entirely? They have given faithful service and they have got nothing by way of bonus. Surely to goodness, if we are striving for good labour relations in this country, the first one to set an example should be the government itself in treating its employees fairly. I cannot understand why a notice was not sent out to all the mail drivers that the government was going to pay a bonus. What is to be done about those who did not get it?

They will get something in the future if the circumstances justify the granting of a bonus in their particular cases. There is no proof whatsoever that some contractors who deserved the bonus did not get it because they were not aware of its existence. When 4,000 got the bonus, people generally hear about these matters.

But does it not seem reasonable that all the mail drivers should have been notified? It is the principle I am talking about. I think it would have been only fair to notify all the mail drivers that a bonus would be paid. The Postmaster General says that a bonus is to be paid in the future if the circumstances justify it. I should like to know if any consideration will be given in the way of extra payment to those rural mail drivers who, owing to bad weather in the winter and to muddy roads in the
Postal Service

spring, cannot cover their route by the ordinary road but go a certain distance and then have to retrace their steps and complete their round by another road. Is there to be any extra pay for that extra driving?

In cases of that kind we pay an honorarium after we have ascertained all the facts, and found that the drivers have to do quite a lot of work which they did not contemplate when the contract was signed.
Mr. fjTEITIENSON: Again I ask, have the mail drivers been notified that they will be paid this extra amount for extra driving during bad weather and road conditions, or is this just another case where only those who know about it and apply will get the extra money?
We pay them when they make a claim, if it is justified. They come to learn their business, like everybody else.

Yes, much to their own sorrow. I am talking of the principle and saying that all the mail drivers should be informed of what is intended so that we shall not have the poor fellows who do not know anything about it not getting any extra pay. It is only reasonable, if they do this extra work, that they should be paid extra for it, and they should be notified accordingly. Have they been notified to that effect?
No.

As one general to another, I have a feeling for the Postmaster General. I must say that I admire his courage in his desire to have this large amount of money put in his hands to spend at his own discretion. I never had any such grand opportunities when I carried that title myself.
I am a little bit concerned regarding some of these rural mail couriers being given a war bonus while others are not given that war bonus. I think the issue has been somewhat confused this afternoon by a technical term referred to as a yardstick. It has been asked, could we not find a yardstick by which these rural mail couriers could be paid on the same basis? I am going to suggest to the Postmaster General that he adopt the military term of a point system and allow a certain number of points for various considerations which would entitle a courier to get an increase in his war bonus. Very successfully the point system was devised to bring the troops back from overseas, and I suggest that it is a no more difficult problem to draw up a point system for the rural mail couriers than one to bring hundreds of thousands of troops back from overseas.

Everyone who has spoken has emphasized the fact that these couriers deserve the war bonus; and if this bill is not passed between now and March 31 I understand that those who are in receipt of the war bonus will lose it. I hope the bill will pass between now and that time. And I suggest that there is plenty of time between now and March 31 for the Postmaster General to produce the information he has been asked to produce.
I asked one question last night, and I do not know whether the Postmaster General is now in a position to answer it. When a contract expires, does the Post Office Department always advertise for new tenders, or does it consider that it is not necessary to put out tenders, provided that the original contractor is satisfied with the contract he has been receiving up to date, either with or without a war bonus, or does the department always advertise when a contract expires?

When a contract expires, if the contractor is giving good service and is satisfied to keep on at the price, whether such price includes the bonus or not, we do not advertise for tenders. Otherwise we advertise.

Will the Postmaster
General give us the assurance that contractors who are writing in now will receive every consideration so that conditions such as those to which I shall refer may not be permitted to continue. In my section of the country I know of an old gentleman on contract who is receiving less than a dollar a day for six hours work each day. He has been carrying the mail for many years, but was reluctant to ask for an increase in his contract price, because he thought he might lose his contract. He and his wife had been trying to eke out an existence through carrying the mail for this amount of less than a dollar a day.
I know of other cases in my constituency where contractors who have appealed to the Postmaster General have been allowed increases in their contracts. I hope the minister will give every consideration to cases similar to the one I first mentioned, where the contractor is receiving as little as a dollar a day for six hours work.
I am sure the representations of the gentleman mentioned would receive a favourable reception. This bill is to meet that sort of condition.

The discussion in this debate has ranged pretty well from Prince Edward Island to Vancouver island and back again, several times, with stops in between. I believe there is but little one could add at

Postal Service
this late hour in the debate. However, I wish to assure the committee that the majority in the house are in favour of the payment of this extra wartime bonus to the mail carriers of Canada.
It is a well known fact that they are one class of public servants in Canada who for many years have been underpaid. As an instance, I should like to record an experience I had a number of years ago when 1 was only a public citizen, and perhaps as such held more prestige in the community than I do at the present time. A friend of mine approached me and asked if I would give him a letter of recommendation. He told me he was tendering for a mail contract running out of the town in which we lived. This was not a door-to-door proposition, but rather one running from town to town. The work on this route necessitated his driving sixteen miles in the morning to a neighbouring town, picking up the mail, driving back to meet a train at 6.12 o'clock in the morning, driving a distance of forty miles, waiting at that point until 3 o'clock in the afternoon and then driving home again, at the conclusion of which his day's work was done-for that day. In performing it he covered about a hundred miles each day. I said to him, "What are you going to get out of this contract?" While I cannot state definitely, I know the price paid was something less than $2,000. I said to this man, "I think you need your head examined more than you need this mail contract."
This only serves to show the type of cutthroat tender system which has been in existence for many years. I cannot suggest a remedy to the minister, because I know of no other way of doing it. But under that system John Jones hears that Bill Smith has a contract for $800, and he thinks that if Bill Smith can do it for $S00 he, John Jones, can do it for $775. He tenders for that amount and gets the contract.
But that is private enterprise. That is what you want, is it not?

I know the minister wants to do everything he can for the mail carriers. After some of us have completed our jobs in parliament, we might find at some stage in the future that we would have to tender for mail contracts. W'hether it be the present Postmaster General or the hon. member for Calgary West who at that time might be minister, I should hope that under either circumstances each would give every consideration to the mail carriers of Canada.
The minister said that this had nothing to do with air mail contracts; is that correct?
Yes.

Then I suggest that the title of the bill should be changed, because it does not say that air mail contracts are not included. I suggest that the title should be "The Rural and Land Mail Delivery Contracts Supplemental Payment Act". I would suggest that title.
We can make that change when we are considering the title.
We are on that section now -"Short title".
I have no objection to accepting the hon. member's suggestion.
I would ask the hon. member to put his amendment in writing.

Mr. Chairman,
while the amendment is being prepared, may I point out again that none on this side of the house is adopting an attitude in opposition to the necessity for the bonus being given to these employees. We are all in agreement. What we are opposed to is the discriminatory power resting in the hands of the minister. We are also opposed to the attitude taken by the minister in, as yet, not being in a position to furnish us with information for which we have asked.

Section 2 of the bill states:
"Mail contract" means a contract relating to the conveyance of mails entered into . . .
In the public accounts four types of mail contracts are listed. There is the rural route contract, the stage contract, the side service and then the city service. Does this bill include these four different types of contracts? If so, what is the city service?

It does
include the four contracts.
What is the city service?
The city service is the contract where the contractor is using multiple equipment.
He uses an automobile in the summer and something else in the winter, or the automobile the year round?
A city contract is a contract where the contractor has a good many pieces of equipment, many trucks; some of them have as many as fifteen which are operated in the city.

Section agreed to.
On section 3

Authorized supplemental payments on mail contracts.

Subsection 2 of section 3 reads:
Payments under a mail contract shall not he supplemented under this section unless the person entitled to payment under the contract makes a written application . . .
Have supplemental payments been made to any contract holders without a written application?
The answer is no.
How is it determined?
I did not understand the question.
I asked the minister whether any mail contractors had their remuneration supplemented without a written application.
I would say that without a request none of them received it, but I do not know if it was always a written request-practically all of them, I suppose.

Why is it that under this section the request must be written? Perhaps I have not made myself clear. Having in mind what the minister said on a previous occasion, namely, that those who made application for increases in remuneration received it after consideration by the department but that those who did not make application did not receive anything, my question is, did any mail contractors receive increases in remuneration without asking for it?
The answer is in the negative.
"Ask and ye shall receive."
Subsection 3 of section 3 provides that a bonus or a supplement will not be paid on a new contract until one year after the contract has come into force. I think that is correct.
Yes.
If a supplement is then asked for and granted does it begin at the time it is asked for and granted, or is it retroactive to an earlier time of the contract?
It would start from the first of the month following the application; it is not retroactive.
Are any of the supplements given now retroactive, or do they begin in the same way?
In the same way.
What is the estimate of the cost of these supplementary accounts?

The hon.
gentleman was not here this afternoon.

I was here part of the time.

There were many questions on this matter and there are still many pending. We are asking for the passage of this bill in order to help the contractors if anything happens which is of the order of what happened during the war when conditions were not stable and when things changed so fast that contractors could not foresee what was going to take place. We do not intend to give any bonuses unless the conditions at the time the bonuses are asked for justify us in coming to the help of these people. I cannot foresee any depression-I hope we shall not have any-but things that I cannot imagine might well come about which would render the carrying out of these contracts by the contractors difficult, I am asking for this measure for one year. Things may happen and we shall have a certain discretion to do this. It -was done during the war and very few people complained about it. It was done as efficiently as it was humanly possible to do it. We intend to do the same thing for one more year. We have received a lot of correspondence from contractors stating that they were glad we were going to do this. They did not want to take the contract without the bonus. They did not like to tender in case they would lose the contract to some other tenderer. If we do not do it there is only one thing we can say. On April 1 we could say, now, you have to take your contract without a bonus or we shall ask for tenders. All the mail contractors have asked us to do this. We are not doing it for patronage purposes or for any other reasons.
Is the minister not going to provide an amount in the estimates to cover this sum; otherwise how is he to get the money ?

We are going to have a certain amount in the estimates; we have to; otherwise we shall not be able to pay the bonus. I may say that we have not yet reached that point, but we may have $1,000,000 or $800,000. I am not yet sure of the amount it will be. I am told that we have enough in the estimates to cover it.
What is the amount?
We have a progressive amount every month. Today I cannot segregate the bonus from the capital which will have to be paid.

Subsection 2 of section 3 of the bill states that no contractor can become eligible for this supplemental payment unless he makes an application. Is the department
	I
going to take any steps to notify these contractors of this provision, or will they have to find out about it themselves?

The law is going to be published. I do not think it would be very" good business for a minister to call on the people to whom he should pay something and have them ask for it. I have not yet made up my mind about the matter.

The carriers in my constituency knew nothing about these bonuses being paid, nor did I as a member of parliament. Will it be made retroactive to any who apply now, having heard for the first time about this Christmas baby bonus?
No.

Then I shall have something more to say about this. I think it is most unfair, because the carriers of British Columbia knew nothing about it and I as a member of parliament was unaware of it. British Columbia may be a long way off but it is still the leading province. I repeat, it is unfair that any carrier who knew nothing about it and consequently failed to make formal application should be penalized while others received it, and any carrier who now puts in his application should receive it retroactively; otherwise it should not be paid at all.

What is the basis upon which refusal to grant the bonus will be made? There must be some yardstick by which the minister refuses to give it to a man who asks for it. What will the minister regard as reasonable or unreasonable in the circumstances?

We do not need a yardstick for that. It was explained at length that we had no yardstick either for refusing to grant it or for granting it. God has endowed the officials of this department perhaps with more brains than the ordinary man on the street, or at least with just as much; and, with the experience that the officials have had, surely they will know whether an application is reasonable or not, and the word "reasonable" still exists. If it is not reasonable to grant it we shall simply tell the man who asks for it that it cannot be given. Suppose a man carries mail from the station to the post office a distance of a mile and a half or half a mile and carries it either in a wheelbarrow or on his back; we shall not grant the bonus.

That is just the point. A line must be drawn somewhere; otherwise how could you determine the matter. Sometimes a second tender is called, for the reason

Postal Service
that the first tender was too high. Where is your line? What basis will you go on? I know one case of 1,180 yards where the trip is made twenty-four times a week and the man received a bonus of 100 per cent. Had he asked for 200 per cent or 150 per cent, would he have received it?
Those are questions to which generally we do not reply.
That is true.

It is the same as if I asked the hon. gentleman whether he wanted to buy a house and how much he would pay for it, and asked him, if the gentleman who had the house for sale wanted 100 per cent more for it, would he pay it or would he not? The hon. gentleman would use the bright intellect that Providence has given him and make a reasonable decision. The same applies to our officials.
It might make a difference whether I was using my own money or that of somebody else.
Anyone who uses money that is entrusted to him is obliged to use his judgment, just as much as if he were spending his own money.
May I ask the minister this question. Were the members notified about the possibility of carriers applying for the bonus?
From now on they will be notified.
But were they last year?
They were notified through the publication of the order in council, which was done legally.

But there are fifty thousand orders in council and I cannot read them all. I would not have time. Apparently the members were not notified that carriers could apply. May I ask a second question? What procedure must the carrier follow in order to make application for this bonus? Can a member make application on behalf of any carrier in his riding?
Certainly.
Then I am making application right now for every carrier in my riding.

We are now getting some insight into the basis on which these things are being done. It would appear that the 83166-44
Postmaster General is inclined to throw up his hands and sit back and leave it to Providence. From the information we have been able to get in the house tonight one might be justified in assuming that Providence would make a better job of it than the Postmaster General has done.
No doubt about it.

But unfortunately Providence does not reveal its workings to all of us. I suggest that we need some information from the Postmaster General, assuming that he is master of his own actions. In answer to a question by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, he began to say that there is in the estimates a fund to provide for payment of bonuses. He did not complete his answer but said something about 8800,000 and something to the effect that we have a progressive system. Will he please tell us what arrangements have been made to provide for this money and whether it will be included in the estimates?

I do not know whether this is the right place to discuss it, but there is in the estimates a progressive amount which is so much a month'. It is around $10 million in all and we draw on that amount. We always have at the end of the year a little more than we need. In our estimates we have foreseen, that we would have a certain amount of bonuses to pay and it is included in that amount.
The Postmaster General speaks of having always a little more money than is needed. These bonuses have been payable, I understand, only since 1942. What disposition is made of the surplus?
The surplus remains in the hands of the Receiver General of Canada. We do not draw it; that is all.
That seems to be a fairly catch-as-catch-can method of accounting.
Oh, no. It has been the method of accounting ever since 1867 at any rate, whether we were in power or some other party.

Not having been here since 1867, I cannot contradict the Postmaster General on that point, but I very much doubt whether that has been the generally accepted method of accounting, and that may be one reason why the auditor general himself does not appear to have been able to find this item and call attention to it in the public accounts.

Postal Service

But there are certain other questions which I think we might put to the Postmaster General in order to see if we cannot arrive at a formula basis on which to put this fund and on which to administer it. It would surely be desirable to arrive at a percentage basis for this bonus. On the assumption that the contracts, when first awarded, were fair and that the department took into consideration the mileage, the number of boxes, the difficulty of the route and so on when receiving tenders, and that the amount which was first authorized was a fair payment for that route, what would be the objection to saying that, now that the cost of servicing the route has increased, we should simply arrive at a percentage of the cost increase, or a percentage represented by that increase, and apply that percentage all across the board? Would there be any objection to that?
I should very much like to do it in that way; it would be very simple; but unfortunately we have to take realities into consideration, and they do not allow of its being done in that way.
What are the realities?

If we have to value a contract, for example, which is being operated in the peninsula of Essex where all roads are beautiful and, where there is no snow, there are very few factors to increase the value of the contract. But if we have to value a contract which is being operated in a district where the roads are bad in winter and summer, especially during a winter like the one we are having, surely the cost to the contractor in those parts where the snow is deep would be much more than it would be during a winter like the one we had last year.
Yes, bute-

I am sorry, but I am not through. In addition to that, there are many other factors which I cannot give to the hon. member offhand. Labour is getting scarce. I hope that labour will not continue to be as scarce as it is now. Automobiles are perhaps costing more than they should; they are difficult to get, and so forth. All these factors have to be taken into consideration in valuing the bonus. The hon. member is surely able to visualize them just as well as anyone else.

What I wish to point out is that the government, particularly when answering criticism from the official opposition, do not hesitate to give us a hard and fast figure or percentage of the increase in the cost of living. If they can give it as readily as that

on those occasions. I can see no reason why they cannot assess it on this occasion. To deal specifically with the point raised by the Postmaster General, he spoke of the different circumstances governing different routes which would tend to make the increase in, cost different again for the different routes. Surely the different circumstances were all taken into consideration in awarding the first contract, or when the tenderer submitted his first tender.
The cost consideration was not taken into acount when we asked for tenders; It must have been taken into consideration by the man who was putting in his tender.

That is admitted. But
the point I am trying to make is that these factors were taken into consideration and one could say therefore, or should be able to say that the contracts or tenders as originally agreed to represented a fair price for the carrying of the mail over that particular route. If you do not accept that principle, then you say the whole thing is on an unsound basis. So, accepting that principle for the moment, one goes on to argue in this way, that the cost of living and the other factors which make up the increased cost of the delivery of mail are the same over the whole country. The increase in the cost is what I am talking about: the increase in the price of tires, the increase in the price of cars and perhaps in the price of gasoline, and various other things which the carrier needs. The proportion of this increase is the same over the whole country. The original differences were taken into account when the contract was first let. So I suggest that, if one wished, one could say the percentage increase is perhaps thirty per cent; one could fix that and then say, "We will increase our contract by thirty per cent". If it was a contract for 81,000, and that was a contract which took into consideration the difficulty of the route, the depth of the snow and all those factors which the Postmaster General referred to, the contract would be increased by thirty per cent; and a smaller contract for an easier route would be increased by the same percentage. So you would still be carrying forward the difference which governed you in arriving at the different contracts, and the situation would be fair across the whole country. I suggest that system would be so much better than leaving it arbitrarily to the Postmaster General that I would ask him to give a further explanation as to why some such system cannot be adopted.

Postal Service

I wish to say a few words supplemental to what the hon. member for Kamloops has said. We do not want to go on asking questions unendingly and just for the sake of being a nuisance. However, I suspect-though I am not very familiar with the minister's background in detail-that he must have once been a sportsman because I think he is quietly trying to tire us out. It seems to me that this proposition, when one comes to consider it, is most astounding. As far as I know, it does not enter into any of our business dealings in any other way. It seems to me that the proposal made by the hon. member for Lake Centre last night was, on the face of it, most reasonable. After saying that there was no excuse for parliament to grant this power, he was asked by the hon. member for Mackenzie, "What do you suggest as an alternative?" This is what he said in reply:
This is a very proper question. I suggest that, if the present rates are too low-and I believe in most cases they are-then, grant the bonus to all, and place all in the same position.
I take the same ground as that taken by the hon. member for Kamloops. If you are going to inquire into 8,000 contracts and try to consider whether or not the man was compos mentis when he made his tender, surely that is a most astonishing undertaking for the minister to step into. It seems to me to be quite contrary to common sense. Also, as has been well pointed out by the hon. member for Lake Centre, it is contrary to all the sound precedents for government expenditure. It seems to me that the minister has not answered the question of the hon. member for Kamloops and he has not answered what the hon. member for Lake Centre said last night, that these people should be treated the same all across the board. I cannot for the life of me see why that should not be done, and I think, if the minister wants to carry this bill quickly, he might take some pains to explain that to us. I do not think he has done so.

We have been discussing this matter for quite a long time, and I thought I had explained it. Of these contracts, there are a certain number of contractors who are not asking for anything. They do not need anything; they have not asked for anything, and I am sure they will not ask.
Oh, oh.

Well, that is the fact. I will give the details for which the hon. member asked. There is to be a list of people who did not ask for anything, people 83106-44J
who do not live very far away, people who live in a district where they receive a newspaper and things like that, and they have not asked. We want to help these gentlemen. There are two ways. We have made provision that on March 31, if these contractors do not want to renew their contracts at the pre-war price or rather at the old price without the bonus, because there is no bonus in these cases, we are going to ask for tenders and they may tender any amount they wish. If they are the lowest tenderer, they will get the contract, provided that this contract is at a reasonable price, because we have the same right as any party asking for a tender. We are not bound to take the lowest tender, unless the tenderer is competent and his rate is reasonable. We know that conditions have been unsettled for some time and that some contractors are losing money. If they come to us and show that they are losing money we shall give them a bonus. The bonus varies. It may run from S50 to S400 in some cases. It all depends upon the contract. Where there is a long mileage and difficult roads to cover we sometimes give a larger bonus. If the committee does not want us to give this bonus we can strike out this clause, but this question has been studied for years and years in this department and we know that, to be absolutely fair, there cannot be any other yardstick than the amount of the tender. The man who is tendering must know something about the conditions before he tenders. He must know the route and the difficulties, the temperatures likely to be experienced the year round, and base his tender accordingly. Some tender for a small price because they carry passengers and merchandise.
That is the point.
Yes. That is done principally on the long routes in British Columbia. When an application is made for a bonus we have to make inquiries and consider all these factors.
You are not paying a bonus; you are renegotiating 8,000 contracts; is that it?
We are not going to renegotiate 8,000 contracts unless we are approached.
But if any of the 8,000 come to you, you will renegotiate?

Why does the hon. member say that we will renegotiate? We will study the question and renegotiate if
Postal Service

it seems reasonable to do so, and we can only do that for one year. All that is done in accordance with the principle of this bill.

The length of time during which this debate over what appeared to be an unimportant bill has dragged on since last night would suggest that members in all sections of the house are dissatisfied with this policy.
No.
The hon. member for Eraser Valley offered strong objection and so did the hon. member for Springfield this afternoon.
Quite a number among your own people are satisfied.

I think it is unreasonable to expect the men who are hauling the mails to know of the existence of orders in councils which have been passed at the rate of from twenty-five to thirty a day. During the present session, my desk mate the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre asked questions about orders in council which the ministers of the departments concerned apparently did not know had been passed. I think we are certain to find that these 8,000 mail couriers in Canada will have a just complaint. Let me remind the committee of the language of section 3 of this bill:
Notwithstanding the Post Office Act but subject to this act, when in his opinion the public interest will be promoted thereby, the Postmaster General may authorize payments required to be made under a mail contract to be supplemented for the duration of the contract, out of moneys provided by parliament, by such amount as the Postmaster General may determine but not exceeding the amount required to increase the payments under such mail contract . . .
We are being asked to vote upwards of one million dollars to be handed over to the Postmaster General to be spent on these terms. Personally I have the greatest respect for the Postmaster General and for his judgment, but I think it is unfair to ask parliament to vote one million dollars to be spent on these terms. I think the proposals made by the hon. member for Kamloops and the hon. member for Lake Centre are reasonable. Of course we want to vote the one million dollars, but let us spend it on a mileage basis or on the basis of the number of boxes serv ed or on a percentage basis, so that all of the 14.000 will receive some benefit from this one million dollar melon which is to be sliced. Unless the Postmaster General can give us some more satisfactory answers, I think we shall be here for a long time yet.
IMr. E. Bertrand.]

Hon. members have spoken of a certain amount that is to be spent at the discretion of the minister. There is in the budget of every minister a certain amount of money which he has the right to spend at his discretion. A minister, for example, may let a contract for less than $5,000 without having to call for tenders, and few of these bonuses would reach that amount. Last year, when my estimates were before the house I said that I intended to ask for an amendment to the Post Office Act which would give the minister the right to award contracts for the amount of S500 without having to ask for tenders. The amount now fixed in the law is $200, and that dates back to 1867, but $200 in 1867 was probably worth more money than $500 is today. I was reproached by the hon. member for Peel on February 12 for having said that and not then bringing down legislation accordingly. The truth is that I intended to bring in a bill, but upon reflection I thought that if I were to increase the amount to $500 there would be unfortunate reactions in the house, and so I did not present the bill. I do not want to be reproached on both accounts, for spending too much and for not asking for sufficient money.
Last evening I asked the minister in how many cases the lowest or any tender had not been accepted.
I can get that information.
That was the purpose of my question last night.
Nobody can foresee all the questions that bright brains like those I see before me may ask.
That is why I put my question on Hansard last night.
But I can easily find that out. I would say it would run about two dozen, according to the information I received from my officials.

I have always felt that my constituency was distinguished because we seem to have got a fair share of this particular kind of attention in Stanstead. There the department has called for tenders not once but several times and the contracts have not been let.

I remember an occasion when we called three times. That shows the amount of care we take with the taxpayers' money.

Postal Service
How soon will the department arrive at the conclusion that, where there are a number of tenders and the lowest figure is not accepted, there must be something wrong with the appraisal of the tenders.

Not necessarily. I shall give an example. There is a rural route in the county of Labelle, represented by my hon. friend who sits near me. They asked for an amount to which we could not agree. We did not want to renew and give the bonus that was asked, because it was too high. We have asked for tenders twice and the bids have been so 'high we have refused. The route is without a delivery system at the present time. However, we expect to find someone who will take it at a reasonable amount. The amount was more than double, so we refused it.

I am not going to insist further, but I hope the minister will have a little time over the week-end to look after these unfortunate people in Stanstead who are receiving such indifferent service, owing to the difficulty with respect to tenders.

I wish to ask one brief and simple question, which does not require study. I am referring to the answer given by the minister to the question asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario. I understood the minister to say that if a mail carrier carried passengers or freight, this was taken into consideration, and that there was a reduction in his contract for carrying mail. Did I understand the minister correctly?

I meant to say that if he comes for a bonus, saying that he is losing money, he will certainly be questioned as to whether or not he is transporting passengers, and the amount that he is making from that.
For example, I have before me one contract respecting Kamloops and Merritt, British Columbia, where there are six trips a week, seventy-three miles each way at a cost of $1,475 a year. That is a stage service. As hon. members know, the stage service is carried on in coaches, and passengers are carried as well.
I notice that the minister and. his assistant had a little difficulty with that question, so that they will understand my difficulty in getting this in my mind with clarity. But I wish to know-

The hon.
member is abusing the fact that I did not read the figures properly the first time.

Let me
apologize at once for whatever I did-and I do not know what it was. But in order to keep the record straight, what I am trying to find out is this: I gathered.-
Read it again.
I did not hear that, either.
It does not matter.

This is not like the mule and the man, one kicking the other. However, I will consider where that came from.
But what I have in my mind is this: Did I correctly gather the statement made by the minister when I understand that if a person carrying mail cared to improve his position by carrying passengers, freight or parcels, this would be taken into consideration in fixing the amount of his mail contract?
He makes a tender.

Perhaps I had better finish what I am saying. It may be that I am getting deaf at my age. But if that be the principle, then it is a wrong one, because it penalizes a man who tries to improve himself by his work.

No; there is one factor the hon. member is forgetting. The man who has the contract has fixed his price by tender. He knew someone else was going to tender. He would realize that somebody else was supposed to tender from the fact that we were asking for a contract, to be let by tender. He.must have known he would carry a certain number of passengers, for which he would be paid, and that would-most certainly have affected the amount of his tender.
When he comes for an increase we have his price on which he has operated for some time; we have also the rate of the other tenders which were submitted, and generally we know whether or not they are transporting, passengers. It would be quite unfair to treat them as if they were not making money from carrying passengers, and to give them the bonus which they would not deserve, because they had received money, which was reflected in their tenders in place of that bonus when they were operating before.

I explained that yesterday.
Mr. Chairman-
Oh, oh.

I am glad to hear these sounds of approval. subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS

speechtext:
Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Secretary of State for the Prime Minister) moved the second reading of Bill No. 18, to readjust representation in the House of Commons.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), in introducing this bill, indicated that it was intended to refer it, after it had received second reading, to a special committee to be set up to consider and recommend the boundaries of the constituencies to be adopted. Owing to the amendments to the British North America Act which have been brought in since the last time redistribution took place in this country, I think I should place on the record a list of the changes which have taken place before we go into the matter of redistribution again this year.
As hon. members will realize, this is the eighth occasion on which a redistribution bill has been introduced since the formation of our confederation. As hon. members are well aware, the provisions of the British North America Act provides that, on the completion of each decennial census, the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons shall be readjusted.
Hon. members will recall that in July, 1943, owing to the fact that this country was at war, a humble address was presented to His Majesty the King praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to provide that, notwithstanding the provisions of the British North America Act 1867 to 1940, it should not be necessary to readjust the representation of the provinces in the House of Commons in consequence of the completion of the decennial census taken in 1941, until the first session of parliament commencing after the cessation of hostilities between Canada, Germany, Japan and Italy. That amendment to the British North America Act was passed by the parliament of the United Kingdom on July 22, 1943.
Again in May, 1946, this house approved a further humble address being presented to His Majesty the King, praying that a measure be laid before the parliament of the United Kingdom to provide for the readjustment of representation in the House of Commons on the basis of the population of Canada. This measure was passed by the parliament of the

Redistribution
United Kingdom on July 26, 1946, and by it section 51 of the British North America Act, 1867, was repealed, and a new section 51 substituted. The new section provided that the number of members of the House of Commons shall be 255 and that the representation of the provinces thereafter should be determined upon a proportionate basis in accordance with the rules contained in the amended section.
I should also like to refer to an act which was passed at the last session of parliament, known as "An act to amend the Quebec Boundaries Extension Act, 1912''. As the then Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) pointed out at the time, in 1912 parliament passed several acts to extend northwards the boundaries of Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba. In the bill dealing with the extension northward of the boundaries of Quebec, it was provided that the population of the added territory would not be counted in the population to be divided by sixty-five to find the unit of representation on redistribution of the membership of this house. In view of the fact that the population of Quebec is no longer a determining factor in fixing that representation, it was considered that the restrictions which had been inserted
The bill, as passed by parliament on June 24, 1946, provided that the act should not come into force until proclaimed, and should not be proclaimed unless and until there is concurrent legislation of the legislature of Quebec. I am informed that such concurrent legislation has not yet been passed, and consequently, in considering the population of Quebec for the purpose of redistribution, it is necessary to omit from our calculations the population of the area added to northern Quebec, numbering 3,067. However, as the Minister of Justice pointed out at that time, this number is so small in relation to the total population of Canada that it does not effect in any material way the unit of representation.
Dealing with the provisions of this bill, I may say that it is introduced in the form that has been adopted since 1903. In this form, redistribution bills have been introduced by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Sir Robert Borden, our present Prime Minister, and Mr. Bennett. The bill is, of course, not identical with the previous bills, owing to the fact that the number of constituencies is now fixed, and not subject to change.
Section 7 of the bill is new. providing for the preparation of maps as soon as possible after the passing of the act. Previously maps were required but no authority existed for their preparation.
Section 8, while it provides that the act will take effect only upon the dissolution of the present parliament, makes provision for the immediate appointment of such returning officers as may be required, pursuant to section 8 of the Dominion Elections Act, 1938.
In the Representation Act of 1933, no provision was made for the appointment of returning officers, and it was necessary to pass an amending act in 1934 to provide for their appointment, prior to the dissolution of parliament. In previous years, before 1925, returning officers had not been appointed on a permanent basis and were appointed only for the conduct of a single election.
The new section 51 of the British North America Act 1867 to 1946 is printed in the explanatory notes of this bill, and for purposes of record I would ask leave to have this section included in the record of this debate.

I have already stated that this bill is in the form that has been presented for the past forty-four years, it being left to the house to determine the boundaries of the constituencies, rather than to have a bill introduced containing proposed boundaries for the constituencies.
The advantages of this procedure were fully dealt with by our Prime Minister when he introduced a similar bill in 1923, and I do not think any good purpose will be served by repeating the statements he made at that time.
I might perhaps quote Mr. Bennett when, in 1932, in introducing the bill of that year, he stated:
The old contest in the House of Commons over the boundaries of constituencies which represented the views of the government of the day, has not taken place since 1903.
When the bill has been read a second time it is proposed to move that it be referred to a special committee, composed of representatives of all parties and groups in this house. This committee will be charged with the responsibility of delineating the boundaries of each electoral constituency. Subject to the right of the committee of the whole, or of the house, to make such amendments as may appear desirable, the schedule is incorporated in the bill and, upon its final approval, forms part of it.
In the past, several guiding principles have been followed by similar committees. As far as possible, county and municipal organizations have been followed in defining the boundaries of constituencies. In addition, it has been the uniform practice for many years to provide that the unit of representation in large cities should be larger than in rural constituencies. In other words, the population of an urban constituency should be considerably greater than for a rural one.

Redistribution

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
That is
left for the committee to determine. The reason for this was so well expressed in the debate on the redistribution bill in 1933 by our Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, that I can do no better than quote his words on the second reading of the bill, as reported in Hansard, page 1590:
If it were not so, with the country as sparsely settled as it is in some parts, the rural constituencies would be difficult to control for purposes of administration. But there is a further and more important reason, and that is that as far as the urban constituencies are concerned, they have a means of voicing public opinion which x-ural constituencies have not. I need not mention the various organizations which exist in the urban centres, the large number of bodies such as boards of trade and commercial, industrial and social organizations, all of which play a part in forming and expressing public opinion. But I would refer particularly to the effect of the press. The daily press of the country is for the most part, if not exclusively, to be found only in urban centres. The rural press is, generally speaking, weekly, semi-weekly or bimonthly, and the press from the cities finds its way into the country districts to a very great extent, whereas the same cannot be said to be true of the press of the rural parts. As hon. members will know there is no other single factor that so largely goes to influence public opinion as the press. What is done in that way is reflected again by what is said here'on the part of hon. members.
He continued:
There is a further reason also, which I think will be apparent and which will appeal to hon. members. It not infrequently happens that rural constituencies are represented in the House of Commons by gentlemen who reside in cities and urban municipalities, but the reverse, except in very rare instances, is not the case. It seldom happens that an urban constituency is represented by someone who resides the year round in a rural constituency, but there are in the house at the present time and have been in all previous parliaments, many hon. members who have represented rural constituencies but who are more familiar with the life of the cities and the large towns than with the life and needs of the rural communities. The principle of a larger unit for urban representation has been accepted practically ever since confederation by committees which have dealt with this matter, and I hope and assume full recognition of it will be given by the committee to which this bill will be referred.
I mention these principles because it cannot be expected that redistribution can or should be carried out with mathematical accuracy.
Finally, 1 may say, again referring back to past history, that since the new method has been adopted of referring the question of delineating the constituencies to a special committee of the house, agreement has usually been arrived at, owing to the fact that a real effort was made by all members of the committees to be fair, just and reasonable. I have
every confidence that the same spirit of justice and fair play will be displayed by those who form the committee this year.

subtopic: READJUSTMENT OF REPRESENTATION IN THE HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister who has moved the second reading of the bill has said, this bill stands in the name of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). It was introduced and given its first reading on his motion. I am sure I voice the sentiments of all hon. members when I say I regret the illness of the Prime Minister and hope that his recovery will be speedy, and that 'he will soon be restored to health and strength to take his place as leader of the house, where he is so much missed.
Because of the Prime Minister's illness, I have not had an opportunity of discussing one phase of the bill with him. I doubt if he understood what the effect of the wording of part of the bill would mean to the electors in one section of Canada, and I doubt very much if he would want that part of the measure to become law. As it now stands, if it is enacted in its present form it creates an impossible constituency. It is impractical; it is inappropriate; it is improper; it is unfair to the people it effects, and I am sure it is disappointing to the people of the Mackenzie district which the bill seeks to add to the constituency of Yukon.
Let us look into the conditions in the Yukon and Mackenzie districts. Section 2 of the bill sets out the number of members each province shall have, and then it goes on to say that there shall be one for the Yukon territory. If it were allowed to stand at that it would be all right; but these words are added:
. . . including the Mackenzie district of the Northwest Territories.
Redistribution

What does that mean? I venture to say that very few members of the house realize the enormity of those words. At the 1941 census Yukon had a population of 3,174 whites, while the Mackenzie district had a population of only 2,113. It is now estimated that the Yukon territory and the Mackenzie district each have a population of about 5,000 whites. I think that is overestimated. I do not believe either has that many.
What about the area? The area of the Yukon territory is 207,076 square miles, while that of the Mackenzie district is 527,490 square miles. In effect this bill creates a constituency 734,560 square miles in size. Does anyone think one member can properly represent a constituency of that size? It is an impossibility. Great Britain, from John o'Groats to Land's End is only 88,745 square miles. The constituency now sought to be created is eight times the size of Great Britain; yet Great Britain sends over 600 members to its parliament. Here we have one constituency, eight times the size of Great Britain, to be represented by one member. I ask hon. members if that is not ridiculous. I say it cannot be done. I am afraid the minister sponsoring the bill does not greatly care whether it can be done or not.
The Yukon territory and the Mackenzie district are separated by a range of mountains; they have nothing in common, and there is no communication between those two sections of Canada. The only way to travel from one to the other is by plane. Think of the expense of conducting an election campaign by plane. The returning officer would have to have a plane, and his deputy returning officers as well as the candidates would have to have planes. A candidate would have to charter a plane: and one would not be enough, if he were to carry on a proper campaign in a constituency of that size. I know what it costs in a comparatively small area, because in Yukon it cost me nearly $1,500 to charter a plane in the last election. That would be only a drop in	the	bucket	to what	it would cost	tocampaign [DOT] this constituency. The population in the Yukon territory and in the Mackenzie district is entitled to representation in the House of Commons. In its wisdom, away back in 1901 or 1902 the government decided it would be wise to give Yukon representation in	the	house.	Millions	upon millions	of
dollars worth of gold were beginning to pour out of that territory. The output in gold has now reached the enormous sum of $300,000,000.
A ukon has been a splendid market for millions upon millions of dollars worth of Canadian produce. We import everything we use: machinery, clothing and food. All those 
things are sold there. The government of that day showed its wisdom when it gave Yukon representation in the house, so that it might have a member here, regardless of political affiliation, who would be familiar with conditions in that far country and could be of assistance to the government. I believe every member Yukon has had, regardless of political affiliations, has been of assistance to ministers whose duty it has been to administer the government of that area.
Dawson City is the centre of the gold district, and at that point is found the oldest producing placer gold camp in the world. The one big company operating there, and still mining placer gold, has its campaign worked out for the next twenty-five years; and in each of those years they will take out millions of dollars, even if nothing new is found. Those large sums can still be taken from the old workings.
I say Yukon is entitled to better treatment from the government than it is getting in this bill. If the government wished to give the Mackenzie district, with its area of 527,490 square miles, representation in the House of Commons, it would have been more appropriate to have extended north the boundaries of some of the most northerly constituencies in the prairie provinces. That would have been a natural extension.
In British Columbia, for instance, the constituency of Cariboo could have been extended to the north. In Alberta, either Peace River or Afchabaska could have gone farther north, as a natural growth, just as the minister said tonight that the provinces of Manitoba, Ontario and Quebec were extended, to the north.
In Saskatchewan, the constituencies of North Battleford, Prince Albert, Melfort and Mackenzie border on the Mackenzie district, and could be extended north; give them a slice of it, if it is not desired to tie it all on to one of them. But even if that were done, it would be more appropriate than to attempt to tie it on to the Yukon territory.
What is the Mackenzie district? What gives it its importance? Why has it not had representation before? The reason is that a few years ago gold was found at Yellowknife, and a stampede wTas started. Thousands of people went in there and staked thousands of wildcat claims. So far as I am aware, out of all those claims that were staked there are only two producing mines. It has proven a bonanza for the mining brokers of the city of Toronto who have deluged everyone, including hon. members of this house, with their literature

Redistribution
advising them to buy these wildcat mining stocks. That is no reason why the Mackenzie should be hooked on to Yukon.
How did this come about? Last summer the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) and some of his staff made a trip by plane, the only way they could make it, into the Yellowknife. The people of the Yellowknife have been asking for representation in parliament, and -what is the result? They are sloughing them off on Yukon. If you want to give them representation in parliament, tie them on to some appropriate constituency. You could not get a more inappropriate arrangement than to tie them on to Yukon.
The minister made that trip at public expense, which is quite proper for a minister of the government. If he had had to go at his own expense he would realize what an election will cost there. In 1930, a similar bill was introduced. By Bill No. 13 of seventeen years ago it was proposed to add to Yukon constituency, not only the Mackenzie district but all of the northwest territories, those three large districts. That would have meant that the constituency would extend from Alaska on the west, to the Atlantic ocean on the east and to the north pole on the north. That was a wonderful piece of legislation, and this one is not much better, by only a few thousand miles. They realized the difficulties when Bill No. 13 was introduced in 1930 because they provided:
If, in the opinion of the chief electoral officer, the day fixed for the poll at a general election is such that resort by the returning officer to such means of transportation as must be resorted to for the proper conduct of an election in the electoral district of the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories would involve undue risk, he may, notwithstanding anything in the Dominion Elections Act, fix a subsequent day for the poll in the said electoral district and a day for the close of nominations shall be determined accordingly.
The anticipated trouble then, and the weather is not any better today, seventeen years later. Let us look at the explanatory note to that bill. It reads:
The purpose of this bill is to combine in a single electoral district the Yukon Territories and the Northwest Territories, the latter not now being included in any electoral district. Sections 1, 2 and 4 of the bill are self-explanatory. Section 3 is necessary owing to the difficulty of communications between the basins of the Mackenzie and the Yukon rivers.
The Yukon drains all the northwest section of this continent and flows into the Bering sea opposite Siberia, while the Mackenzie drains the centre of the continent of North America. The explanatory notes continue:
In whatever part of the electoral district the returning officer has his headquarters he can conduct the election only by flying from one part of it to the other. His presence in each from time to time will be essential to give opportunity for the making of nominations, and the ballots will, as things now stand, require to be printed at Dawson and transported by air to such polls in the Northwest Territories as it is found possible to provide for in the fourteen days which intervene between the close of nominations and the holding of the poll. At certain times of the year, particularly when the ice is forming or breaking up, flying becomes impossible, and without making some provision such as that contained in section 3 the inclusion of the whole of the area in a single electoral district might be entirely illusory.
It is just as illusory tonight as it was seventeen years ago. I shall be disappointed if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), who sponsored this bill, is still willing to put this upon these people when he understands the conditions. It is not his nature to be unfair; it is his nature to be just. All I ask is a fair deal for these people. I hope the committee to which the bill is to be referred will understand the situation and be fair. When the bill comes back to the committee of the whole I hope that a reasonable and proper amendment will be accepted.
I cannot better describe the section of the bill to which I have referred than to say that it is outrageous legislation, the iniquity of which could not be overstated. That portion of the bill seeking to form one constituency out of Yukon and the Mackenzie district is a legislative abortion. I warn the minister that, although it is a legislative abortion, so far as I am concerned it will not be still-born.

May I say just a word in support of the grievance the previous speaker has presented to the house. When this matter was up for discussion at the time we had before us the resolution to Westminster asking for an amendment of the British North America Act, hon. members of this group pointed out at that time how unfair it was to make one constituency across the whole of the North American continent, as the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Black) has just described it. However, my purpose in rising was to speak on one phase of the matter that is before us.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Gibson) pointed out, rather commendably I would say, the whole story of the amendment of the British North America Act and the principles that now govern redistribution among the provinces. But during the course of his remarks, not only did he tell us that it was intended to refer the bill to a special com-
Redistribution

mittee of the house, but he seemed to take it for granted that that procedure would not be questioned. The Secretary of State quoted the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he spoke in 1923 to the effect that the method of referring this matter to a committee had proved to be satisfactory and was even commendable. I would remind the Secretary of State and hon. members on the opposite side of the house that more recently the Prime Minister has indicated his belief that some day we must get away from this outworn method which we have followed these many years. A few weeks ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) asked the Prime Minister where he stood on the matter, and he replied that it was still his opinion that it would be better to refer the matter to a judicial or independent commission than to a committee of the house. He stated that the reason he was not following his own judgment in the matter was that he felt it was the wish of the majority of the house to continue the old practice. He went on to say, and I quote from Hansard:
I hope, however, the day will come when the House of Commons of Canada will see the wisdom of allowing its redistribution to be made by some impartial tribunal and not by the members of the house themselves dealing with the matter in committee as it has been dealt with in former years.
These words of the Prime Minister were spoken in the house on February 3 of this year as recorded at page 68 of Hansard.
The Secretary of State referred not only to the previous position of the Prime Minister back in 1923, but also quoted from Mr. Bennett who was prime minister at the time of the last distribution who used words to the effect that in his view at that time it was perfectly satisfactory to refer the matter to a committee of the house. I was not here at the time and do not know what went on in the special committee or in the house after the report was brought in, but I cannot help but notice the strange results of the work of that committee, especially in terms of the wide variation in population in different constituencies. In my own province, for example-and I shall refer to the population figures of 1931, although I have the figures for 1941 before me, because the redistribution last made was on the basis of the 1931 population figures-the rural constituencies-I will not complicate the matter by making any comparisons with urban constituencies like my own-varied all the way from Souris with a population of 25,000 to Selkirk with a population of 52,000. Similarly in Ontario the variation in rural constituencies ran all the

way from 18,000 for the constituency of Glengarry to 88,000 for the constituency of Nipis-sing.
I have also found it very interesting to notice that a number of constituencies which seemed to have been traditionally Tory, at the time of the last redistribution, were carved out in such a way as to include a rather small population. My genial friend who sits near me, the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser), represents a constituency the population of which in 1931 was only 37,000. The constituency of Hastings-Peter-borough had a population of only 27,000. On the other hand, if we go into the Niagara peninsula where at that time the tradition was a little more on the other side of the fence, we find a constituency like Welland with a population at that time of 82,000.

liical matters of procedure around the house, and that it should be regarded as a function of the House of Commons as a whole to decide what method is to be followed.
I believe it would be a good idea to test the view of the house as to whether we want to continue the outworn method of referring the carving up of the provinces to a committee of the house or whether we want to see the wisdom to use the Prime Minister's words, of referring it to an independent tribunal. He expressed the view that he thought the majority wanted to follow the old method. Well, here is an opportunity to find out whether this house wants to carry on with old, wornout method, or see the wisdom of referring the matter to an independent tribunal.

I rise to say a word with respect to this amendment, largely because on a former occasion I was instrumental in introducing, on the part of the government of the day, a resolution calling for the setting up of a committee, one of the duties of which would be to study:
. . . methods used to effect a redistribution of electoral districts in Canada and in other countries and to make suggestions to the house in connection therewith.
I refer the house to Hansard of March 13, 1939, at page 1807.
In introducing that resolution, I urged that up to that time redistribution committees had been remarkable rather for the lack of harmony which had resulted from their deliberations than for any just appreciation of the work of the committee. As 'has been said by the minister who introduced the bill, up to 1903, I believe it was, the government of the day simply came before the house and introduced a bill in which the constituencies in Canada were laid down. In 1903, there were parliamentary committees on which were members from all sides of the house. My recollection is that in 1924 the committee

brought down a report to which very little objection was raised. Members who were in this house in 1934 will remember that the committee pretty well ended up in what might have been called an unseemly turmoil, with the result that in 1939 the government of the day thought some study andi exploration might be made into some system whereby we would get away from this eternal wrangling and where perhaps the interest of the electors themselves rather than of interested members of parliament might prevail.
In introducing that resolution, I pointed out that it would be advisable at some time or another to introduce a bill to provide for the appointment of a redistribution commission. The committee of that year made a thorough study of methods of redistribution and instructed Mr. Harry Butcher, the committee counsel, to report to them as to the methods in effect in other countries to bring about a fair and equitable redistribution of the constituencies in those countries. I need not say to any hon. members who know Mr. Butcher that he is a man of the highest personal integrity and was recognized by members on all sides of the house as being perfectly impartial in his view. The committee, after having heard Mr. Butcher's statement, reported as follows; as will be found at page 3810 of Hansard of May 10, 1939:
Your committee gave consideration to the methods in use in Great Britain, Australia. New Zealand, the Union of South Africa and in the United States, together with suggestions-made by the counsel as to how redistribution could be effected in Canada.
Your committee, however, concluded that there are many important questions, including that of the relation of urban to rural population, as it may be affected by the next decennial census, that should receive detailed study before a definite decision is made.
Your committee there submits, without further comment, a statement of the methods employed in other countries, and the suggestions made, for the consideration of the house.
I am sorry to say that I have no clear recollection of the discussions which took place, but evidently this report appealed to the government of the day because I have in my hand-and I found it in an old file in my possession-a bill entitled, "An Act to provide for the appointment of a redistribution commission". The first reading was to be in May, 1940, and it was to have been introduced by myself as postmaster general. This bill provided that a commission should be set up. May I say in passing that I do not think the bill was ever introduced. Members of the house will remember that in May, 1940, the phony war ended and we had other things to think of than looking after our own particular

Redistribution
internal quarrels. The bill provided for the setting up of a commission to consist of three commissioners, the chairman to be a judge of a superior court and two assistant commissioners to be appointed in each province. Apparently those commissioners were to sit only in the province from which they came. The commission was to travel all over the country, was to hear witnesses in the different localities, and then was to report to the secretary, of state. May I immediately point out some of the difficulties that will arise should we appoint such a commission, difficulties which were not quite so apparent at the time this bill was drafted and at the time it was intended to bring it before the house as a government measure. One of the difficulties of which we took some .account at the time was in connection with the kind of instructions which would be given to this commission.
I notice that certain instructions were given under the duties of the commissioners, in section 9 of this bill:
In the preparation of a bill for the redistribution of a province into electoral districts the commission shall give due consideration to:
(a)	The physical features;
(b)	Means of communication;
(c)	Existing boundaries of electoral districts, both provincial and federal;
(d)	Boundaries of administrative areas;
(e)	Such other pertinent factors as may occur to it or to which its attention may be drawn.
One of these pertinent factors, not to mention them all, was what proportion in the way of population there should be-or disproportion, I should perhaps say-as between rural and urban areas. Ever since confederation, it has been generally conceded on all sides and by all political parties that the rural member should represent a somewhat smaller number of population than the city member. The reasons are fairly obvious. They existed to a greater extent in the old days when the means of communication were not so easy; but they still exist even today, because the opinion in a small congested area is very much more easily ascertainable than that in a very large area. The bill was to have been sent to a committee.
It was then considered that in all probability consideration should be given by the commissioners to such things, for instance, as homogeneity of interest in any given constituency ; homogeneity of occupational interest, let us say. If a certain section of a city or town were largely populated by those who were engaged in manual labour, in all probability some consideration should be given to a constituency allowed to elect someone who would perhaps more truly represent the views of labour than a person who came from a constituency in which there were large numbers
who owned residences in a higher bracket. There was, and there always has been- although it does not exist to the same extent in certain of the older provinces-consideration of the ethnic or, to put it more crudely, the racial situation. My hon. friend the member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) knows that in the eastern townships for many years, on all sides it was considered advisable to have smaller constituencies in order that the English-speaking population might have a greater chance to be represented. That was due in large degree to the generosity of our French-Canadian compatriots, but all political groups were in agreement that it should be done. I see my hon. friend the member for Argenteuil (Mr. Heon) in his place. He knows that Argenteuil was at one time the smallest rural constituency in Canada. They have a population, if I remember rightly, of something like nineteen thousand. It was kept as a small constituency for the purpose of giving representation to the English-speaking population of that district.
Mr. HEON; Which was 39-5 per cent, according to the latest figures.
Mr. POWER; Yes. In Ontario in certain sections, I believe, similar considerations weighed with the leaders of poltical parties when redistribution was being made.
